articles.title_orig: Breaking | US, China trade chiefs hold call ahead of Trump-Xi summit in Shenzhen
articles.title_zh: Breaking | US, China trade chiefs hold call ahead of Trump-Xi summit in Shenzhen
articles.content_orig:
US Treasury secretary presses Beijing to honour commitments made in Busan as Washington raises concerns over recent Chinese actions
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Trade Representative Jamieson Greer held a phone call with Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng on Friday as both sides moved to finalise preparations for President Donald Trump’s planned meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Shenzhen later this month.
“Secretary Bessent emphasised the importance of China fully and immediately implementing its commitments made in Busan and raised concerns about recent Chinese actions,” a statement from the Treasury Department said.
“He underscored that continued progress depends on concrete results and that the United States will closely assess China’s implementation of the arrangement.”

articles.title_zh: White House said Starlink donated its service, but tax dollars are funding it
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
The Trump administration quietly paid Elon Musk's SpaceX nearly $1.2 million in government contracts, despite previously characterizing the services as a “gift,” according to a report.
SpaceX was handed four contracts from March 2025 to June this year for Starlink services provided to the White House Communications Agency, a military unit responsible for managing secure comms for the president and executive officials, The Washington Post r eports.
The contracts amount to nearly $1.2 million, but in March last year, White House officials said that Starlink “donated” the service, per a New York Times report that has resurfaced.
“The gift had been vetted by the lawyer overseeing ethics issues in the White House Counsel’s Office,” the Times report stated, citing a White House official.
Three of the payments totalling $502,000 were reported last week by the legal advocacy group Democracy Defenders Fund. A fourth contract worth $686,000 was identified by the Post .
“I’m very concerned,” Virginia Canter, chief counsel at the Democracy Defenders Fund, told the Post . “We worry about pay-to-play access and these kinds of transactional arrangements. When someone is given this access and subsequently given these government contracts, you have to wonder if these government contracts are in the best interest of the taxpayer.”
Starlink beams broadband internet to millions of customers in the U.S. using thousands of satellites in low-Earth orbit. There were security concerns about the installation of Starlink’s services at the White House at the time.
Then-White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said the work was to “improve Wi-Fi connectivity on the complex” at the time.
The Independent has contacted the White House and the Pentagon, which paid for the services, and SpaceX for comment.
In its damning report, Democracy Defenders Fund alleged that in the 17 months since Musk publicly split with President Donald Trump, he has seen his net worth more than double, and his companies have netted at least $10 billion in new government contracts.
The revelation about the SpaceX contracts comes as Musk suffered a humiliating defeat in the midterms after he poured $500 million into Republican midterm campaigns to no avail.
“Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” Musk reacted on his X platform. “Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn’t work this time.”

articles.title_orig: Panda fans flock to Zoo Atlanta for the debut of Ping Ping and Fu Shuang
articles.title_zh: Panda fans flock to Zoo Atlanta for the debut of Ping Ping and Fu Shuang
articles.content_orig:
The six-year-old male and female duo arrived in the US from China under a 10-year loan agreement
Zoo Atlanta’s newest pandas munched bamboo and lounged on Friday during their public debut as smiling visitors lined up to welcome them.
Ping Ping, a male, and Fu Shuang, a female, arrived in September from China under a 10-year loan agreement, bringing the cuddly black-and-white bears back to the zoo after a two-year absence.
After spending the past weeks getting acclimated to their habitat, the six-year-old pandas greeted visitors in the newly renovated Arthur M. Blank Panda Grove.

articles.title_orig: Hegseth calls US-Iran war a 'courageous and historic effort'
articles.title_zh: Hegseth calls US-Iran war a 'courageous and historic effort'
articles.content_orig:
Iran has stepped up diplomatic efforts amid suggestions by United States President Donald Trump that the US could resume full-scale strikes on Iran.
The US news website Axios quoted a US official saying that US Central Command (CENTCOM) was preparing for the resumption of major military operations in Iran, and that it was just waiting on orders from Washington. On Thursday, Trump told reporters the US may have to “destroy” the rest of Iran, adding that people will “know soon enough” if he acts.
Tehran’s intensified diplomatic push comes after Iran downed two US reconnaissance drones near Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, which the US struck earlier this week. Iran says it will retaliate if the US resumes larger strikes.
On Thursday, Iran offered the US a new nuclear and peace proposal via Qatari mediators, to be discussed only after Washington meets Tehran’s seven demands, a senior Iranian official told Reuters. The US is examining the proposal, Reuters reported.
Iran has made meeting its seven demands a condition for reopening the Strait of Hormuz and restarting peace talks, including on its nuclear programme. The demands include the lifting of sanctions on Iran, the unfreezing of Iranian assets and the end to the US naval blockade of its ports in and around the Strait of Hormuz, among other things.
It has also stepped up ties with Russia, with its top security official, Mohsen Rezaei, travelling to Moscow for talks on Thursday. During that visit, Rezaei said: “On the issue of diplomacy, we have announced seven conditions ⁠to the Americans. As long as they do ⁠not execute our seven conditions, we will neither open the Strait of Hormuz nor have negotiations.”
Meanwhile, the US has insisted a deal on Iran’s nuclear capacity must be part of any ceasefire agreement before wider peace talks can restart.
On Thursday, Rezaei met with Russian President Vladimir Putin at the Kremlin to deliver a message from Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei. Iranian state media did not elaborate on ⁠the contents of the message.
Rezaei called it “an extremely important exchange” according to remarks reported by the Iranian embassy, but also did not give further details.
However, The Financial Times reported that Russia previously agreed to supply Iran with 90 helicopter-mounted launchers for precision-guided missiles, despite needing its own weapons for the Ukraine war. The newspaper cited a Russian defence manufacturer’s production schedule for 2024 and 2025, which it has examined, showing an order for helicopter-mounted launchers being assigned a code used to refer to Iran in Russian defence documents.
Relations between Russia and Iran have deepened since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and during the US-Israeli war on Iran that saw the two countries become the most heavily sanctioned in the world. Iran has provided Shahed drones, which Russia has modified and used heavily against Ukraine.
In return, Russia has also reportedly helped Iran develop supersonic cruise missiles, sold it Verba shoulder-launched anti-air missiles and shared information with Tehran potentially relevant to nuclear weapons.
“It is indicative of Russia’s willingness to continue supplying Iran despite its own wartime demands and with far less concern about Western objections than in the past,” Nicole Grajewski, a non-resident scholar at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, told the FT.
In early October, Putin said Russia was prepared to take part in mediation to bring an end to the war .
Images released by the Kremlin showed its foreign affairs adviser Yuri Ushakov and chief of the Russian military intelligence, Igor Kostyukov, attending a meeting with Iran’s security chief alongside Putin.
The meeting also strengthened Iran’s economic ties with Russia.
“During the meeting with Mr Vladimir Putin, discussions were held regarding the construction of gas pipelines from Russia to Iran,” said Rezaei, Iranian state TV reported.
He said the gas pipelines would address Iran’s gas shortages and facilitate the sale of Russian energy to neighbouring countries.
Tehran said Iran’s natural gas refineries had been hit during the most intense phase of US-Israeli strikes on Iran earlier this year, which lasted 40 days.
Separately, Russia’s Foreign Ministry advised citizens against travel to Iran “In light of the remaining risks of a new escalation around Iran”.
During the most intense fighting of the war, Iran struck bases in Gulf countries hosting US military assets, as well as civil and energy facilities and infrastructure.
Senior Iranian officials have repeatedly warned that any state helping the US to target the Islamic republic will be a “legitimate target” should US attacks resume.
On Thursday, Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi held phone calls with several Gulf leaders, including the foreign minister of the UAE, Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan.
They discussed regional developments as well as diplomatic efforts for stability in the region, according to Araghchi’s Telegram channel.
Araghchi spoke with Saudi Foreign Minister Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud about efforts to improve security and stability in the region, according to the Saudi foreign ministry.
Araghchi also discussed de-escalation efforts with the foreign ministers of Kuwait and Turkiye.
In a separate call, Araghchi talked with Qatar’s Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani about coordinating to reduce tensions, the Qatari foreign ministry said.
Sheikh Mohammed stressed support for efforts to secure freedom of maritime navigation.
In a statement, Oman’s foreign ministry said the safety of passage through the Strait of Hormuz was a main topic of discussions, in a call between Araghchi and Oman’s foreign minister.
Iran continues to tightly control shipping lanes through the strait, where several ships have been damaged in recent days. It has granted exemptions to shipping restrictions to Iraq and Qatar, in the Gulf region, as well as to India and China.
Despite his Republican Party suffering a drubbing in this week’s US midterm elections – largely because of public anger over the war on Iran and the resulting rise in energy prices – US President Donald Trump has refused to rule out further strikes on Iran.
On Thursday, Trump told reporters at the Oval Office that he may have to “destroy the rest” of Iran.
Former Iranian diplomat Hadi Afghahi told Al Jazeera that Tehran can ease the path to a settlement if the US also shows flexibility. He argued that Trump “really does not want to go to war, because war again will cost him more”. However, the US president’s next move is unpredictable, observers say.
Afghahi cautioned that Trump “is still surrounded by a group of hawks”, including the energy and treasury secretaries.
Trump has shown willingness to engage in diplomacy, however. Qatar’s ⁠Emir ⁠Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad ⁠Al Thani discussed diplomatic ⁠efforts to ease regional tensions in a ‌phone call with Trump on Friday, according to the Qatari Emiri Diwan.
The leaders reviewed international diplomatic efforts, including the Doha-led mediation efforts to support negotiations in recent weeks, in a bid to reach “a comprehensive agreement that puts an end to the crisis”, the Diwan said in a statement.
Tehran warned it will retaliate on a wider scale than it has done so far if the US resumes the war. It has also said talks will become unfeasible.
Iranian officials said Iran has the capacity to strike further than the Gulf using weapons manufactured in Iran.
On Thursday, a spokesman for the Supreme Advisor to the Commander of the Aerospace Force of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said: “In the event of a new aggression, any country or force that helps America attack Iran can be a legitimate target of the Islamic Republic.”

articles.title_orig: Paraguay’s Peña loses top aides as impeachment trial resumes over failed bank
articles.title_zh: Paraguay’s Peña loses top aides as impeachment trial resumes over failed bank
articles.content_orig:
Paraguay’s president impeached amid bank collapse crisis
Paraguay’s President Santiago Pena is facing impeachment following the collapse of Ueno Bank, a major digital bank, which has plunged the South American country into its deepest political crisis in more than a decade.
Pena announced his resignation on Thursday, but politicians formally filed impeachment charges against the president. Pena, a former International Monetary Fund (IMF) economist, then requested a 72-hour extension to present his defence at an impeachment hearing, because he had been given less than 12 hours to answer “an accusatory writ and about 300 pages of attachments”, adding: “That is not due process.”
However, the Senate convened a rare session on Friday to consider Pena’s political future, opting to move forward with efforts to remove him from office.
Until March 2025, Pena held a stake in Grupo Vazquez, the parent company that owns Ueno Bank.
Ueno Bank was established in 1976 and remained a small financial operation for decades.
After being granted a full banking licence in 2023, it rebranded and grew to become a household name in Paraguay within five years. Customers were incentivised with cashback offers on groceries and it built a network of more than 70 branches. The bank sponsored Paraguay’s national football team and its name was plastered across the country’s main stadium.
Ueno bank reported that it had 3 million customers, roughly 60 percent of Paraguay’s adult population.
The digital bank managed $800m of public funds, including about $380m invested by Paraguay’s state pension and health fund, according to data from the Central Bank of Paraguay.
On Monday, Paraguay’s central bank decided to put Ueno bank into resolution – the strongest action it can take short of placing the bank into liquidation – after finding that its solvency ratio, a measure of its capital against its risk-weighted assets, had dropped to less than half of the legal requirement.
Resolution allows regulators to transfer a failing bank’s deposits to other institutions before liquidating remaining assets.
Customer accounts were frozen, leaving millions of depositors, retirees and workers scrambling to recoup their savings and unpaid wages.
Ueno Bank’s nearly 3 million customers still cannot withdraw cash, make digital payments or use their bank cards.
“Santiago Pena and the Colorado Party have stolen all our savings,” said Luis Pineda, one of the protesters marching to Congress on Wednesday. “We are fed up with 70 years of plunder,” he added, an apparent reference to the right-wing Colorado Party which has ruled Paraguay almost uninterrupted for more than seven decades.
Regulators at Paraguay’s central bank found a pattern of risky lending to “insiders”, reported ABC Color, a leading Paraguayan newspaper. This means that executives or major investors of a bank have approved questionable, low-security loans for themselves, their families or their own businesses. In this case, Ueno had loaned $146m to companies tied to its owner, Grupo Vasquez, which has links to Paraguay’s president.
Investigators found loaned amounts went beyond legal limits and were not backed up by enough collateral to cover the debts if they went bad.
Central Bank regulators found Ueno’s loans to companies linked to its owners were poorly documented while the bank had wrongly counted some expenses as assets.
Once the books were corrected, Ueno’s capital, the cushion banks must keep to absorb losses, was revealed to be less than half the legal minimum.
Protesters blame President Pena personally for the crisis because of his ties to the failed bank. Until recently, he held a financial stake in Ueno Bank’s parent holding company. After taking office in 2023, Pena appointed the former head of Ueno’s predecessor company, Carlos Carvallo, to head the country’s central bank, giving an insider the role of overseeing the institution. Carvallo has resigned from his position.
Pena denies any improper ties to the bank.
Protesters also say they are unhappy that so much public pension money was invested with the bank under Pena despite warnings about its high-risk insider lending practices.
Paraguay’s Congress rushed through a law on Wednesday, providing a state-guaranteed fund for repaying depositors within five business days, starting on Thursday with small accounts holding up to $1,600.
The fund insures up to about $36,000 per customer, which the central bank says will cover the full balances of an estimated 97 percent of customers.
Paraguay’s Public Prosector’s office has ordered multiple criminal investigations. On Thursday, a judge ordered six Ueno executives, including founder Miguel Vazquez and bank President Juan Manuel Gustale, to be detained pending trial, while two others were placed under house arrest. In all, prosecutors have charged 27 bank officials and associates with breach of trust and attempted fraud.
Paraguay’s President Santiago Pena has tried to step down and wants Congress to approve his resignation. However, opposition politicians want him to be formally removed from office rather than merely allowing him to resign. They argue that allowing Pena to step down would preserve his eligibility to become a senator for life and shield him from possible prosecution.
Paraguay’s Attorney General Emiliano Rolon Fernandez has ordered three criminal investigations into the Ueno Bank crisis, including allegations involving Pena and other current and former government officials, the prosecutor’s office said on Thursday.
The investigations will examine authorities’ oversight of the bank, their handling of its failure and the placement of public funds in the lender.
No. Paraguay has a long history of bank failures and went through a prolonged banking crisis from the mid-1990s to the early 2000s.
In 1995, the central bank was forced to close Bancopar, which had severe liquidity problems and had also practised insider lending to companies linked to the bank’s owners. Three more banks also failed because of risky practices and poor oversight. The government was forced to cover the deposits of customers of all four banks, causing lasting damage to public confidence in Paraguay’s banking system.
Other banks including Banco General, and Banco Aleman were closed in this era. Banco Union and the state-linked Banco Nacional de Trabajadores and Banco Plus also failed.
Banco Espirito Santo in Portugal collapsed in 2014 with losses of $4.8bn when it was revealed that the family-controlled banking group had hidden losses. The Bank of Portugal had to split and rescue what was the country’s second largest private bank. That happened as Portugal was recovering from a deep recession, austerity cuts and bail-out obligations to the International Monetary Fund (IMF), the European Central Bank (ECB) and the European Commission.
In 2008, the three major commercial banks in Iceland – Glitnir, Kaupthing and Landsbanki – all collapsed within days following the bankruptcy of Lehman Brothers. The three banks were heavily exposed because they had borrowed from foreign capital markets far too aggressively. Iceland did not shore up the banks, instead seeking help from the IMF and launching criminal investigations.
The collapse of Lehman Brothers triggered banking crises in other countries, including the United Kingdom, but banks there were mostly propped up or rescued by governments.
Fraud and insider lending caused the collapse of Banco Intercontinental Baninter in the Dominican Republic in 2003 with losses of $2.2bn.
And in 1991, Bank of Credit and Commerce International, a globally active bank, collapsed with losses of $10bn. Extensive fraud, hidden bad loans, and illicit operations masked the true scale of the deficit until the intervention of regulators. It was shut it down simultaneously in more than 70 countries.

articles.title_orig: Poised for breakout moment in Latin America, Pope Leo also faces test of health
articles.title_zh: Poised for breakout moment in Latin America, Pope Leo also faces test of health
articles.content_orig:
Pilgrims depart in the pouring rain Oct. 3, 2026, from the St. Cajetan shrine in Buenos Aires on the annual pilgrimage to Luján, home of the national patroness and where Pope Leo XIV will visit Nov. 11. (David Agren)
Send your thoughts to Letters to the Editor . Learn more
Pope Leo XIV arrives in Argentina, the homeland of Pope Francis, Nov. 8, the middle stop of an 11-day trip to South America that starts today (Nov. 6) in Uruguay and ends Nov. 17 in Peru. The trip marks a homecoming of sorts for the U.S.-born pope, who served twice as an Augustinian missionary in Peru and was later appointed bishop of Chiclayo.
Francis never made a homecoming to Argentina after his 2013 election, though he twice flew over the national territory on trips to Paraguay and Chile. He also never explained his reasons for not returning, though priests and pundits attribute his absence to a preference for avoiding the country's deep social divisions and messy politics.
"He was a pope who, unfortunately and unintentionally, got caught up in our notorious social and political divide," said Sergio Berensztein, an Argentine pollster and political analyst. "He likely paid a political price for that. The fact that Francis decided not to visit Argentina has, in turn, contributed to people losing some of the initial fervor they once felt for him."
Opinions about Francis seemingly depend on social status, political orientation and geography —  with many Argentines seeing the pontiff as much a political actor as a pastor and failing to appreciate the gravity of Archbishop Jorge Mario Bergoglio being elected the first Latin American pope.
"He is remembered with great affection. In general, ordinary people, those who truly hold values, appreciate him," said Fr. José María di Paola, a prominent cura villero , the description given to priests backed by Francis, who work in the country's shantytowns. "This is true all over the world. People who seek war are selfish; naturally, they are unable to appreciate his message."
Signs of the enduring affection for Francis and his legacy were on display at the Oct. 27-28 meeting of popular movements that took place in suburban Buenos Aires. Participants hailed from groups that included parish soup kitchen staff, cartoneros (who pick recyclables from municipal trash bins) and a ministry working on drug addiction in the country's shantytowns.
A drone view shows people gathered outside the Buenos Aires Metropolitan Cathedral in Argentina April 26, 2025, for a memorial Mass for Pope Francis, formerly Argentine Cardinal Jorge Mario Bergoglio, who died April 21 at age 88. (OSV News/Reuters/Stringer)
The participants ambled along bumpy roads through a shantytown in Ciudad Evita, a suburb named for the former Argentine first lady, Evita Perón, wife of former President Juan Domingo Perón, whose Peronist movement spoke of social justice and labor rights.
The event ended with a pilgrimage to the aptly named " Ciudad Papa Francisco ," (Pope Francis City), a community center founded by the curas villeros .
Many recalled the inspiration and support provided by the Argentine-born pope, who prioritized the poor and peripheries as archbishop of Buenos Aires and later as leader of the universal church.
"In working-class neighborhoods, (soccer star Diego) Maradona acts as a unifying symbol; similarly, Francis fosters unity. However, among the more affluent, this image of Francis does not carry the same weight," said Ariel Malvestiti, a staff member of Familia Grande Hogar de Cristo , a ministry that supports addiction recovery.
"Perhaps he didn't change their lives as significantly as he did for the poor because he spoke to the poor in their own language, and he spoke directly to them," Malvestiti added.
People pray at a Mass celebrated Oct. 28, 2026, to conclude the Regional Meeting of Popular Movements in suburban Buenos Aires. Pope Francis championed the gathering of grassroots organizations, which work in downtrodden parts of Argentina. (David Agren)
It's another story in more affluent parts of Buenos Aires, where images of  Francis are rarely spotted — unlike the murals of Maradona and Lionel Messi, who led Argentina to World Cup success. Francis' message of social justice and support for the curas villeros — who are perceived as being aligned with Argentina's national-populist movement known as Peronism (something they deny) — caused many to see the late pope as much a politician as a pastor, according to observers.
"Almost all of his gestures and actions … were instead interpreted through the lens of local politics and social dynamics. It was as if (he) was still the archbishop of Buenos Aires, rather than Pope Francis," Fernando Domínguez Sardou, professor at the UNIE University in Spain, said in a 2025 interview . "His gestures and deeds were, above all, rooted in the spirit of 'turning the other cheek' and engaging in direct acts of charity, rather than being driven by the logic of local politics."
He added, "The pope was unable to bridge the ' grieta ' — the political divide and social polarization in Argentina — "nor was he able to transcend it."
" La grieta " or the crack, splits Argentina politically into Peronist and non-Peronist camps.
Its existence was immediately visible after  Francis' election, when the ruling Peronists and then-President Cristina Fernández de Kirchner — who the then-Archbishop Bergoglio of Buenos Aires criticized for alleged corruption and mismanagement of poverty issues — failed to immediately congratulate the new pope. Peronists, however, quickly blanketed the city with posters of Bergoglio reading, "Argentine and Peronist." Francis and Fernández de Kirchner became friendly — a gesture angering non-Peronists, who later seethed when the pope appeared glum in a 2016 photo with non-Peronist President Mauricio Macri.
Argentina's president Javier Milei , who won in 2023 despite badmouthing Francis, has enthusiastically embraced Leo's upcoming visit. The president is expected to greet the pontiff on the tarmac as the papal plane arrives in the afternoon Nov. 8. The federal government has declared a statutory holiday nationally for the pope's arrival and locally in the cities and provinces he visits.
Pope Francis and Argentine President Javier Milei share a laugh during a private audience at the Vatican Feb. 12, 2024. (CNS/Vatican Media)
But signs of the " grieta " have surfaced — with local media obsessing over which politicians were invited or omitted from Leo's visit to the Casa Rosada, the president's office. The Peronist government of Buenos Aires Province, a Peronist stronghold containing the capital's working-class suburbs and many shantytowns, is also mobilizing people for the pope's visit to Luján, home to the shrine to the national patroness, Our Lady of Luján.
"They are convinced … the pope will deliver a message centered on social justice, not just in Luján, but throughout his various visits," said Mariano De Vedia, who writes on the intersection of politics and religion for the Argentine daily, La Nación. "They're looking to contribute by helping to ensure a massive turnout, thereby providing greater support and wider exposure for the pope's appearance."
Priests point to signs of a strong social interest in Leo's visit to Argentina. An annual pilgrimage last month from Buenos Aires to Luján drew an estimated 2.7 million participants.
"People possess a faith and a spirituality that extend beyond the institutional sphere," said Fr.  Roberto Ferrari, who is part of the group Priests for the Option for the Poor. "During times of crisis, people turn to the church or take part in pilgrimages," he added.
But the politics surrounding the visit remain messy, along with attempts to appropriate the pope's legacy. Archbishop Jorge García Cuerva of Buenos Aires has called for unity ahead of the papal visit.

Kombos says Ankara has spent decades violating Cyprus’ sovereignty while invoking the UN Charter against others, calling the gap between Turkey’s ‘words and deeds’ stark.
The Trump State Department denounced the recent eastern Mediterranean maritime agreement between NATO member Turkey and the fractured Libyan state.
The Turkey-Libya deal has also caused frustration and anger among many nations because they say it rewrote the established sea borders of the sensitive Mediterranean Sea region, where large deposits of gas might be located.
The Eastern Libyan parliament approved the maritime accord in mid-October. The region is ruled by military leader Khalifa Haftar, who has formed an alliance with Turkey — the maritime deal ignores Libya’s internationally recognized government in Tripoli in the northwestern part of the oil-rich country.
A U.S. State Department spokesperson told Fox News Digital: "The announcement of the ratification of the Turkish-Libyan delimitation memorandum of understanding has raised tensions in the region and is unhelpful and provocative — and our position on this matter has not changed."

Turkey's President Recep Tayyip Erdogan gives a press conference at the NATO summit on June 25, 2025, in The Hague, Netherlands. (Pierre Crom/Getty Images)
The spokesperson added: "We encourage all countries, including partners in the Eastern Mediterranean, to resolve maritime disputes through good-faith negotiations and avoid any provocative behavior. Greece and Türkiye are both NATO allies . We encourage them to engage bilaterally to address any areas of disagreement."
According to the spokesperson, "Peaceful resolution of such disputes opens the way for commercial investment and exploration that will benefit the entire region."
According to the Turkish news agency Anadolu Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan on Wednesday said the maritime agreement between Turkey and Libya was "entirely legitimate" and not in violation of international law.
He added: "This is an entirely legitimate agreement, both from a legal and a political perspective. There is no need to debate it."
Reuters reported Fidan also shot back at critics of the deal. "There are countries reacting to this. We know why they are reacting. Some are doing so because they need to, some really do have strategic problems with this issue. ​ However, this is an entirely legitimate deal, both from a legal and a statutory perspective. ​There is no need to argue this."
NETANYAHU WARNS TURKEY SHOULD NOT GET F-35S, CITING ERDOĞAN'S HOSTILITY TOWARD NATO ALLIES
Libya's military strongman Khalifa Haftar, center, attends a conference for the country's development and reconstruction on Sept 2024. (Khaled Nasraoui/picture-alliance/dpa/AP Images)
Fox News Digital sought comment from both Turkey and Libya but did not get a response by time of publication.
Greek Minister of Foreign Affairs George Gerapetritis angrily wrote on his ministry’s website that, "The memorandum will not be implemented. And it will not be implemented for the simple reason that it produces no legal effects whatsoever, as it is entirely contrary to international law." He added, "Türkiye had established a system of influence in Libya, essentially seeking to advance its own interests" and the Turkish media has ramped up its anti-Greece rhetoric. "There is a constant stream of reports pushing the Turkish government to become even more aggressive."
Endy Zemenides, the executive director of the Hellenic American Leadership Council, told Fox News Digital that the Turkey-Libya agreement "absolutely" endangers the security of the U.S. and its allies.
He said: "This memorandum specifically infringes on U.S. companies and U.S. energy policy. It effectively denies maritime rights and zones of Crete. Crete is NATO’s southernmost base. And the U.S. has been increasingly relied upon because of wars in the Mideast." He noted that the American companies Exxon and Chevron are present in Crete.
US-BACKED ISRAEL-MOROCCO DEAL DEEPENS ABRAHAM ACCORDS AMID GROWING REGIONAL THREATS
A drilling platform is seen from Larnaca port, in the eastern Mediterranean island of Cyprus. (Petros Karadjias, File/AP)
Zemenides said the Turkey-Libya deal is a way of pushing the U.S. out of the region. The U.S. has not been able to rely on Turkey for a decade, said Zemenides. He continued that "allowing Turkey to challenge the pro-Western order" is not good for American interests.
The European Union invoked unusually strong language targeting the deal, declaring it in violation of maritime law.
"The EU position regarding the MoU is firm and clear. As outlined in the European Council Conclusions of December 2019 and reiterated in June 2025, the Türkiye-Libya Memorandum of Understanding infringes upon the sovereign rights of third States and does not comply with the Law of the Sea. It is null and void and cannot produce any legal consequences for third States."

Israel also blasted Turkey and Libya. The Jewish state has developed a troika alliance with both Greece and Cyprus . Israel’s foreign ministry said on X it "strongly condemns the decision of the Libyan House of Representatives to ratify the Maritime Jurisdiction Memorandum between Turkey and Libya."
Israel’s foreign ministry added on X, "This agreement infringes upon the sovereign rights of our close allies in the region. Regretfully, once again we see Turkey working to destabilize the east Mediterranean region."

articles.title_orig: AI stocks climb after trillions wiped from market values
articles.title_zh: AI stocks climb after trillions wiped from market values
articles.content_orig:
Shares in artificial intelligence and technology firms have been climbing following an enormous sell-off that wiped trillions of dollars off stock values.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq stock index opened higher following a market rout that began in the US on Thursday before spilling over to Asian and European markets into Friday.
Investors had been selling off tech shares in part due to concerns the Democrat victory in the midterm elections would mean slower artificial intelligence development.
However the latest US employment figures added to a mixed picture for American markets on Friday morning, with an unexpectedly strong 165,000 jobs added to the economy in September.
On Thursday, businesses closely linked to artificial intelligence development took a hammering on stock markets, particularly chip and semiconductor makers.
But the Nasdaq Composite opened up on Friday and flattened out around 1.7% higher by lunchtime, reversing some of its 5.5% fall.
The S&P 500, which tracks the share prices of the largest publicly-traded US companies, was around 0.9% higher by lunchtime. The Dow Jones Industrial Average opened a little down before nudging into positive territory.
Nvidia, which shed hundreds of billions in market value on Thursday after shares slid more than 9%, began Friday up more than 6% but settled around 4% higher as trading continued.
SpaceX and Tesla shares, which were also hammered on Thursday, saw more mixed gains, up more than 6% and nearly 5% respectively.
Chipmakers AMD and Micron both dropped by more than 17% on Thursday, but AMD shares had risen by about 12% on Friday while Micron was up more than 8%.
However, stock markets in Asia and Europe fared worse on Friday.
The Kospi in South Korea closed down 6% on Friday, with shares in chipmaker SK Hynix plunging more than 10%. European markets also fell, with the main indexes in Germany, France and Spain ending the day down.
In the UK, the FTSE 100, which tracks the largest companies on the London Stock Exchange, declined 1.01%.
In addition to the recent market volatility, UK traders were also digesting the latest Bank of England decision to raise interest rates and the signal that another rate rise could be on the cards to curb rising prices.
Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said it had been a brutal week for markets, and the key question was whether the jump in the S&P 500 and Nasdaq would be sustained.
"While no-one knows what happens next, it's clear that we've just seen a significant shift in market sentiment," he said.
"Once investors have had the weekend to catch their breath, next week could give a clearer indication of whether the tech trade is going down the pan or fighting back."
The market fluctuations come after the sweeping Democrat victory in the midterm elections.
A number of Democrats campaigned for new rules and regulations for artificial intelligence (AI) and data centres, and the party has since won control of both houses of congress as well as key contests in states that have been part of the AI data centre race.
US President Donald Trump on Friday reiterated his supported for what he calls "super intelligence", saying only "foolish leadership" would "say no to the riches they bring".
However, there have also been concerns over whether the enormous amounts of money being spent on AI will pay off.
Russ Shaw, founder of global tech advocacy firm Tech London Advocates, said the election result was sending a message that a rethink was needed on AI.
"The incoming Congress is going to really focus on AI in a very dramatic way," he told the BBC's Business Today.
"I'm a big fan of AI, but I'm watching what these companies are doing, and they're not communicating effectively at all, particularly in the US, about what the benefits of AI are all about."
He said people were watching firms come into their communities and build data centres while their own energy costs were going up, and those companies "have to be better neighbours".
As well as the fallout of the midterms and the plunge in artificial intelligence stocks, US traders will also be digesting the latest jobs figures.
And those numbers were better than expected: US employers added 165,000 new jobs in October, well above the average monthly increase and more than double what analysts had expected.
Overall the unemployment rate, which counts the number of people who are out of work but actively looking for a job, eased slightly to 4.1% from 4.2% in September .
The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) said the unemployment rate has remained in the narrow range of 4.1% to 4.3% since March.
Neil Birrell, chief investment officer at investment firm Premier Miton, said while the jobs figures may feel like second billing to the market movements they were still important.
"The US economy is running hard which may mean the risks the markets are worrying about at the moment are not such a risk to the real economy as is being feared," he said.

articles.title_orig: To Cross the Red Sea, Shippers Email Houthi Rebels. Read Their Inbox.
articles.title_zh: To Cross the Red Sea, Shippers Email Houthi Rebels. Read Their Inbox.
articles.content_orig:
Captains who wish to transit the Bab al-Mandab Strait have been using a communication channel with the Iran-backed Houthi terror group via email for safe transit, the Wall Street Journal reported on Friday.
While technically the Houthis have said ships not linked to the US, UK, or Israel are allowed through the strait, after the Houthis declared a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia in July, shippers have begun emailing the terror group to receive assurances of their safety.
Emails are sent to an administrative entity established by the Houthis in early 2024 called the Humanitarian Operations Coordination Center, which handles applications and communicates the Houthis actions.
Emails seen by the WSJ show vessels stating that neither the ship nor the crew has any connections with Israel, the US, or the UK.
Ships will share their estimated schedules and assure that they will adhere to the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea.
If the Houthis reply, they will typically do so within the next 24 hours, the WSJ wrote, citing crew members and emails.
In one instance, the Houthis sent authorization to the Chinese containership Zhong Cheng Chang Ling, issuing it a one-week permit and telling it to keep its Automatic Identification System, which broadcasts a ship's identity, position, speed, and destination, in operation through transit.
Additionally, the ship was told to keep VHF Channel 16, a marine VHF radio frequency designated as an international distress frequency, in operation.
The email ends with an invitation to call the HOCC hotline number if needed and to subscribe to the HOCC email alert service to receive news and updates from the Houthis.
The official guidance from international maritime authorities is that vessels should not engage or register with the HOCC, and many vessels choose not to contact them, the WSJ wrote.
However, the captain of the Zhong Cheng Chang Ling told the WSJ that the ship management told him to contact the Houthis as an extra precaution.

articles.title_orig: Where China Sees the Danger in a Wounded Trump
articles.title_zh: Where China Sees the Danger in a Wounded Trump
articles.content_orig:
China won’t be so quick to celebrate the stunning blue wave that washed over President Donald Trump this week.
American voters may have withdrawn the Republican mandate by giving Democrats the keys to Congress, but Trump can still direct his executive powers abroad, even as the opposition prepares to restrain him at home.
After a bruising midterm result for the U.S. president, a wounded Trump may seem like easy pickings for Chinese leader Xi Jinping , who will soon send negotiators to restart trade talks designed to neutralize America’s long-term tariff threat.
Xi had an understanding with Trump and knew what made him tick. But the political setback may make Trump much harder to predict .
Xi spent considerable resources on his rapprochement with Trump, including a state media campaign about Chinese resilience that stopped hostile economic acts by the United States and resulted in two glitzy state visits this year.
A promise to meet Trump at the APEC summit in southern China later this month, and again when Miami hosts the G20 meeting in December, has helped Xi build certainty into China’s relations with its top geopolitical rival.
Beijing may even go as far as to give Trump a foreign policy win at APEC by agreeing to a three-way meeting with Russia’s President Vladimir Putin in host city Shenzhen. Whether Xi makes any concrete commitments there is another question.
“Stability” has been the watchword in China for years, but it has extra weight this year after a campaign of purges swept up dozens of senior figures in elite Chinese politics and the military. Xi’s purges are about corruption in the Chinese Communist Party , but they’re also about loyalty—to him.
A recent gathering of the CCP’s Central Committee had the lowest attendance in over half a century, hinting at the scale of disciplinary action taken ahead of the party’s 21 st national congress in 12 months’ time, when Xi is widely expected to win an uncontested fourth 5-year term.
“Xi’s main political goal now is to secure another term at the 21st Party Congress. That requires not only a firm grip on power but also a case that his continued rule is legitimate and natural,” wrote Christopher Nye, a senior fellow at the Jamestown Foundation think tank.
Xi used the latest gathering of party cadres “to resolve the problems of legitimacy created by the purge,” Nye wrote this week.
A fourth term could extend Xi’s rule over China to 20 years.
So, 2027 will be a delicate year for Xi. He’ll be wary of a Trump unleashed , who, despite being weakened domestically, could channel his energy into foreign policy matters, namely negotiations with China to extend or rip up the Busan truce that kept tariffs at a minimum in exchange for Chinese agricultural purchases and other key commitments.
“Beijing could conclude the election results mean Trump needs an economic agreement more than China does…. In that sense, Beijing could turn Trump’s political setback into a bargaining miscalculation that unsettles the very stability Xi is trying to preserve,” said Craig Singleton, senior director of the China program at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies think tank.
“If Beijing expects last night’s result to humble Trump, it is probably mistaken. He may have less room politically at home, but that could produce even bolder executive action abroad, including new pressure on Chinese companies, tighter economic-security measures and faster reshoring.
"Beijing should be careful about mistaking Trump’s political weakness for restraint in his China policy ."
Trump’s first presidency also began with personal diplomacy with China’s Xi before flattery gave way to full-blown systemic confrontation.
Trump hosted Xi at Mar-a-Lago in spring 2017 and Xi returned the favor in fall with a lavish state visit for Trump in Beijing. The two leaders appeared to agree on $250 billion in commercial deals, which later never materialized.
The trade war followed in 2018, along with the first stage of the tech war that targeted Chinese telecoms giant Huawei the following year. The Phase One trade deal in early 2020 eased tensions but didn’t stop them from boiling over once more during the COVID-19 pandemic.
Beijing was so concerned by the downturn in relations and the mixed signals out of the White House that it feared an “ October surprise ,” a military strike to rally support before Trump’s presidential race with Democrat Joe Biden.
Gen. Mark Milley, then chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, called his Chinese counterpart without Trump’s knowledge to assure him that the U.S. government was planning no such action—and to preempt any miscalculation by Beijing.
Trump’s last experience as a lame duck president didn’t lead to a hot war, but it locked in a new Cold War with China, one of economic decoupling and export controls. And on the last full day of the first Trump administration, his then secretary of state, Mike Pompeo, accused Xi’s government of genocide against Muslims in far-western China.
On the day Biden took office as the new U.S. president, China sanctioned former senior Trump officials in retaliation for the wild final weeks. The message to the new administration, and indeed the expectation, was that Trump’s hard-line China policies should be walked back. That didn’t happen and the rivalry was institutionalized.
Trump has no reason to hold back if Xi doesn’t play ball. And even with Trump neutered, the Democrats may not play nice.

articles.title_orig: Exclusive | Cause of death revealed for 22-year-old who died on LA-bound Southwest flight
articles.title_zh: Exclusive | Cause of death revealed for 22-year-old who died on LA-bound Southwest flight
articles.content_orig:
The cause of death for a 22-year-old man who died aboard a Southwest flight in August has been revealed.
Rain McMillen Walmsley died from the “combined effects of 7-Hydroxymitragynine and Mitragynine,” according to the Los Angeles County Medical Examiner’s Office. His manner of death is listed as an accident.
7-Hydroxymitragynine and Mitragynine are compounds found in kratom, a plant supplement that has drawn growing concern due to recent overdoses.
Kratom comes from a plant native to Southeast Asia, whose leaves are typically dried and consumed for their stimulant or sedative effects, depending on the dosage. In smaller amounts, the substance can produce effects similar to caffeine.
But 7-Hydroxymitragynine, or 7-OH, can produce opioid-like effects when its concentration is artificially increased. Kratom is sold widely, but is legal and unregulated. There’s been recent scrutiny about a high risk of abuse of the drug.
Walmsey was aboard Southwest Airlines Flight 958 on August 7. The flight was traveling from Dallas to Los Angeles when Walmsey suffered a medical emergency and stopped responding.
The biggest news, opinion and culture shaping California right now.
Crew members and fellow passengers attempted to save him, with multiple CPR attempts carried out while the plane continued toward Southern California.
Emergency responders were waiting for the aircraft when it landed at Los Angeles International Airport, but their efforts were unsuccessful.
Paramedics were unable to revive Walmsey, and firefighters pronounced him dead at the scene.
Southwest Airlines previously confirmed that there had been a “medical incident involving a customer” aboard Flight 958 but did not provide additional details about the passenger.
The Irvine City Council, concerned with adverse effects from kratom, recently imposed stricter regulations on the sale and distribution of synthetic kratom. Officials restricted its use to customers 21 and older and established potency limits, banning the sale and distribution of kratom products containing more than 2% 7-OH.
In Mississippi , two college students in separate incidents were found dead with kratom at the scene in September, inflating concern to even higher levels. The Lafayette County Metro Narcotics squad previously said it does “not have confirmed information indicating that kratom or any other substance was a contributing factor in either death.”

articles.title_orig: Zelenskiy, Kyiv mayor trade blame as Russian strikes plunge city into darkness
articles.title_zh: Zelenskiy, Kyiv mayor trade blame as Russian strikes plunge city into darkness
articles.content_orig:
Yemen’s government forces and the Houthi rebel group are trading blame for an attack on the al-Hadara market in the Taiz governorate, that both sides say killed and injured dozens of people.
The Houthis on Friday accused Saudi Arabia, which backs Yemen’s internationally recognised government, of having launched three air strikes on the market, killing at least 30 civilians and injuring eight others.
Its Ministry of Health and Environment in the Yemeni Houthi-controlled capital Sanaa said Riyadh committed a “horrific crime” and called for an independent international investigation into Saudi Arabia’s “systematic targeting” of civilians.
There has been no response so far from the Saudi-led coalition forces. The spokesperson for the Yemeni government forces, Colonel Majed al-Nazili, said the “terrorist” Houthis struck the market with ballistic missiles, causing dozens of civilian casualties. He accused the Iran-backed group of committing a “war crime” and called for accountability.
Al Jazeera could not independently verify the reports.
Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry, reporting from Sanaa, said fighting has been ongoing in the al-Waziiya district where the market is located. The area is controlled by the Houthis, who are also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God).
The Saudi-led coalition has been carrying out attacks on a daily basis to gain control of the district and its strategic mountain range, Mawry said.
“Whoever controls the al-Waziiya district controls the majority of the western Red Sea coastal line,” he added.
The Yemeni army said it recaptured several areas in the Taiz governorate on Friday, including the al-Nidani village, Shaab al-Sarari, large parts of the Sanamat area and the Ribat al-Qarn area in Dhi al-Barh.
Government forces also imposed a siege on entrances to the al-Sarari area, according to the military.
While the Houthis control much of the governorate, the city of Taiz is government-held. An ongoing Houthi siege on the city has lasted for 30 days and affected hundreds of thousands of people in the area.
The United Nations has repeatedly warned of a catastrophe inside Taiz city, where supplies of food and medicine are becoming increasingly scarce.
Yemen’s internationally recognised government launched Operation Dawn of Yemen on October 5  to take control of territories held by Houthi fighters.
Since the start of the military operation, neither Yemen’s government-controlled territories nor Saudi Arabia has been safe from Houthi missile attacks.
The Houthis have been firing missiles and drones daily into Saudi Arabia, hitting oil facilities and disrupting air traffic over the kingdom.

articles.title_orig: Trump Media’s investors lost $2.2 billion while Trump holds $460 million stake
articles.title_zh: Trump Media’s investors lost $2.2 billion while Trump holds $460 million stake
articles.content_orig:
If you’re one of the nearly one million of investors who bought into Donald Trump’s pet crypto coin, the best time to sell was January of 2025, before the whales cashed out and sent prices tumbling. The second best time was yesterday.
Trump’s memecoin has suffered a massive fall-off in the wake of the US midterm elections, tumbling to an all-time-low of $1.12, down from an already paltry $1.70 just prior to the all-important round of voting. Even a month ago, holders of the crypto currency could have gotten out at roughly $2.00 a pop.
Obviously, anybody short-sighted enough to approach Trump coin as an investment is getting pummeled. But with a current market cap of around $340 million, there are clearly more than a few people hoping against hope for a turnaround.
It’s a fitting end for a crypto venture that many had pegged as a grift from the very start. Unfortunately, many more fell for the scam, pumping the coin up to a market cap of $72 billion at its peak.
One analysis found that some 21 well-timed whales pulled the rug on coin holders early into the currency’s launch, getting out with some $214 million and sending the value plummeting.
Predictably, many of the president’s victims count themselves among his biggest fans . In July, the BBC reported that Trump had raked in over $1 billion from all of his crypto dealings combined since returning to the Oval Office in 2025 — money ripped from the hands of the MAGA movement’s most devoted followers.

articles.title_orig: PSA: Want To Learn Link's Ocarina Tunes? Nintendo's Got The Sheet Music For All Of Them
articles.title_zh: PSA: Want To Learn Link's Ocarina Tunes? Nintendo's Got The Sheet Music For All Of Them
articles.content_orig:
Whether you have been playing Ocarina of Time on Switch 2, watching the trailers, or just been in the ether of its release, you almost certainly have an ocarina melody or two stuck in your head right now. For those who want to channel their earworm into a lesson, Nintendo has shared the sheet music for each of Link's in-game tunes, so you can stop whistling Zelda's Lullaby and learn to play it instead.
Nintendo previously announced that it'd share music how-tos via the Zelda Notes app, so you could work out how to play the tunes on any real-world ocarinas you may have accumulated over the years. Of course, you might be waiting to learn any of these until you have one of the official tie-in ocarinas in your hands. Pre-orders for HORI's electric model went live back in September, and we are now seeing orders slowly trickle out for the playable version in select regional Nintendo stores.

articles.title_orig: Taiwan to close representative office in Papua New Guinea, blames China
articles.title_zh: Taiwan to close representative office in Papua New Guinea, blames China
articles.content_orig:
Taiwan says it is closing its representative office in Papua New Guinea and will stop buying liquefied natural gas (LNG) from the country, blaming Chinese political pressure on the South Pacific nation.
Taiwan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said on Friday that Papua New Guinea had repeated previous demands that staff leave its office in the capital, Port Moresby, within a set deadline and had pushed for ⁠its closure.
These actions “reflect China’s continued use of political pressure and economic influence to interfere in other countries’ diplomatic decisions and suppress Taiwan’s international space”, it said in a statement.
China, which claims Taiwan as part of its territory, had welcomed Papua New Guinea’s decision in July to shutter Taiwan’s office in Port Moresby. Taipei rejected the move, and the office remained open in the interim.
The Pacific has long been an area for diplomatic competition between China and Taiwan. Papua New Guinea has formal diplomatic relations with China, but it had allowed Taiwan to have a representative office in Port Moresby.
Taiwan has formal diplomatic ties with only three Pacific Islands nations: Palau, Tuvalu and the Marshall Islands. It also has a representative office in Fiji. Just 12 countries maintain formal ⁠diplomatic ties with Taiwan.
Taiwan previously announced that it had stopped spot purchases of LNG from the South Pacific nation, but on Friday the ministry said it also would no longer sign new spot purchase contracts with the country.
Taiwanese LNG purchases accounted for one-third of Papua New Guinea’s exports.
Last year, Taiwan imported about 8 percent of its natural gas from Port Moresby.
Taipei will also end technical cooperation and assistance programmes, “including medical missions, related scholarship and talent development programmes”, the ministry said.

articles.title_orig: 3 foreign nationals allegedly used AI to mimic CEOs in $129M scheme, DOJ says
articles.title_zh: 3 foreign nationals allegedly used AI to mimic CEOs in $129M scheme, DOJ says
articles.content_orig:
Three foreign nationals have been charged in connection with an alleged international fraud scheme that federal prosecutors say used AI technology to impersonate corporate executives and attorneys and steal more than $129 million.
According to an indictment filed in the Southern District of New York , Jacob Soall, who went by “Rocky Balboa” and “Seba Clarke,” was arrested in Spain in June; Sharon Hazan, who used the nicknames “Superman Cash,” “Impossible Mission,” “Fat Boy” and “Ron,” was arrested in Spain in August; and Guy Sheetrit was arrested in the United Kingdom in September.
All three are accused of participating in a scheme that ran from July 2024 to February 2026 involving the use of artificial intelligence to impersonate the voices and images of corporate executives and attorneys at major law firms to trick employees of several companies into transferring large sums of money to bank accounts controlled by the group, according to a press release from the U.S. attorney’s office.
The trio and their co-conspirators would tell these employees — typically in accounting departments — they needed help with a confidential financial transaction and would use AI technology to mimic the company CEO’s voice, according to the press release.
Then, while pretending to be the CEO, they would tell employees to contact attorneys at large international law firms who they said were also working on the transactions, but in reality, those “attorneys” were also part of the scheme, prosecutors said.
Finally, one of the people involved in the scheme would instruct the employee to wire large amounts of money to bank accounts set up worldwide, according to the press release.
Once the employee wired the money, the group would convert the cash into cryptocurrency “in an attempt to conceal the source, ownership, and control of the stolen proceeds and distribute it amongst themselves and their co-conspirators,” prosecutors said.
The U.S. attorney’s office alleges the scheme stole more than $129 million from companies worldwide, including an investment bank in New York, a hospital system in Missouri, a bank in Rhode Island, a hospital system in California, a financial technology company in the U.K., a mutual fund company in Massachusetts and a pet food company in Florida.
Soall, from Spain and the U.K., impersonated U.K. attorneys and used a script titled “Lawyer Call” to make himself seem like a real attorney when speaking with victims, the release said.
Hazan, from Israel, laundered the money from the scheme, according to the press release. Prosecutors allege that Hazan “boasted that he had been laundering money since 1994; that he had laundered over $400 million in just the past three years; and that, among professional money launderers, he was ‘number one all over the world.’”
Hazan was also convicted of conspiracy to commit bank fraud in the Southern District of New York in 2008.
Sheetrit, from Israel and the United Arab Emirates, is also accused of laundering funds, the press release said.
All three have been charged with conspiracy to commit wire fraud, wire fraud, two counts of aggravated identity theft, money laundering conspiracy and two counts of money laundering. Each of the seven charges carries a maximum prison sentence of 20 years.
“SI technology offers tremendous potential. But the public should recognize that there are some who seek to use this emerging technology to pursue criminal goals,” U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald said in the release, using an abbreviation for super intelligence, the White House’s preferred term for artificial intelligence. “I encourage individuals and the business community to consider how to best protect themselves from the emerging threat of SI-enabled crime.”

articles.title_orig: Denmark’s top court to rule on ‘parallel societies’ after ‘non-western’ people evicted
articles.title_zh: Denmark’s top court to rule on ‘parallel societies’ after ‘non-western’ people evicted
articles.content_orig:
Government claims removal of former residents of housing complex in Helsingør is unrelated to their ethnicity
Denmark’s supreme court is expected to rule on whether the state’s classification of residents with “non-western” backgrounds is covered by racial discrimination law.
The appeal by residents who were evicted from Nøjsomhed-Sydvej in Helsingør, a city north of Copenhagen, could have far-reaching implications for others who have been forced out of their homes by the controversial legislation previously known as the “ghetto law”. The government now refers to affected neighbourhoods as “parallel societies”.
The residents, who have been unsuccessful in other courts, argue that the evictions by the housing association were intended to cut the number of residents with a “non-western” background in order to stop the area from becoming a “ghetto” and therefore subject to the legislation. The government has previously argued the classification is unrelated to ethnicity.
In December, the European court of justice (ECJ) ruled that the legislation may be unlawful . The law requires housing associations to cut not-for-profit housing by 40%, including by selling or demolishing properties or terminating the lease of tenants by 2030.
It also includes demolishing apartment blocks in areas previously labelled “tough ghettos” (now “transformation areas”) by the government, where at least half of residents have a “non-western” background. Other areas with similar socioeconomic conditions – such as high levels of unemployment or crime – are not subject to these measures.
The policy has been widely criticised by human rights groups including Amnesty International. The European Commission Against Racism and Intolerance published a report last month that said there had been “no positive change in the authorities’ approach to the use of the ‘non-western’ category across various laws, policies and administrative practices, including in relation to the ‘parallel society’ legislation”.
The UN committee on the elimination of racial discrimination has called on Danish authorities to stop using the terms “western” and “non-western” in law and policy, and expressed concern that the parallel societies law has a “discriminatory impact on ethnic minorities”.
Residents in Mjølnerparken housing estate in central Copenhagen, who filed a suit against the law in Denmark in 2020 arguing that using their ethnicity to decide where they can live was discriminatory and illegal, have yet to have their case returned to the domestic courts since December’s verdict. More than 1,000 people were forced to move out because of the law.
But legal experts said that the Nøjsomhed-Sydvej case, to be heard on Friday and Monday, could have implications for the Mjølnerparken case because it is likely to lead to a domestic ruling on whether “non-western” background is covered by racial discrimination law.
Susheela Math, the head of legal at the NGO Systemic Justice, said: “If the supreme court decides that ‘non-western’ background is linked to ethnic origin and racial discrimination law, that raises huge questions for the Danish state.”
It would force the Danish state to decide whether it is to abolish the categorisation entirely, which could have ramifications across society, she said.
“[The government] will refer to ethnic origin when it suits them but inside a court, no matter what you present, they say ‘non-western’ background has nothing to do with ethnicity and that they do not collect ethnic data,” said Math.
It is understood that residents of Nøjsomhed-Sydvej would be allowed to return to their homes if they win the case, expected to be decided later this month.
But it is likely to be much more difficult for residents of Mjølnerparken to return to their homes if they win their case when it is heard, because they have been sold.
The Danish ministry of children, senior citizens, and housing has been contacted for comment.

articles.title_orig: OpenAI will keep investing in AI data centers despite election results, CFO tells CNBC
articles.title_zh: OpenAI will keep investing in AI data centers despite election results, CFO tells CNBC
articles.content_orig:
OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar on Friday said the company will continue to invest in artificial intelligence infrastructure, even after voters strongly opposed data centers during Tuesday's midterm elections.
"When I think about the midterms, I need to keep thinking about how do we keep investing to meet that customer demand," Friar told CNBC's Sara Eisen in an interview at the Citi TMT Leadership Summit in Pebble Beach, California. "It starts early with having built relationships with all of the hyperscalers, and it will continue to mean that we raise capital."
Out of 41 local ballot measures across 10 states, voters backed restrictions or rejected pro-development measures in all but one, according to an analysis by Ballotpedia and additional results gathered by CNBC on Wednesday. Opposition to the facilities mounted swiftly over the summer as Americans grew worried about their potential to harm the environment, raise utility bills and contribute to job loss.
Investors have turned skeptical on the AI trade of late due to a combination of higher borrowing costs, concerns about soaring debt and public backlash toward the industry. The Nasdaq on Thursday suffered its steepest drop in 19 months, led by a plunge in shares of the chipmakers and neocloud companies most closely tied to the AI buildout. The stocks rebounded some on Friday.
OpenAI depends on data centers to train its AI models and serve customers, and Friar said she doesn't think the election results dramatically changed anything for the company. On Thursday, OpenAI published a policy blueprint and a series of commitments that it pledged to apply to company-owned and -operated data centers in the future.
"If the midterm means more focus on data centers and communities, we're going to keep doing the work to get into those communities and to build trust with them," Friar said.
OpenAI confidentially filed its prospectus with the Securities and Exchange Commission in June, and Friar said Friday that the company would continue to look into a 2027 debut. Anthropic, OpenAI's chief rival, is trying to go public first, with an aim to hit the Nasdaq in mid-November.
Anthropic's revenue in the first nine months of the year jumped roughly 1,200% to $33.2 billion, according to its prospectus. The company said it has entered into purchase commitments and lease agreements with an aggregate committed spend of about $895.4 billion, "substantially all of which is related to compute and infrastructure."
OpenAI is in talks to raise funding at a $1.25 billion pre-money valuation, Friar said Friday. She said "a good CFO always raises money when she can" and that the round is ongoing.
"The demand for AI is real," Friar said. "I don't think anyone's arguing with that, or if they are, I think it's a losing argument."

articles.title_orig: US job growth surges in October; unemployment rate falls to 4.1%
articles.title_zh: US job growth surges in October; unemployment rate falls to 4.1%
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
The White House says the job market is turning a corner and demand for workers is on the rise.
"Demand for labor is skyrocketing," Kevin Hassett, director of President Trump's National Economic Council, said in an interview, noting that not only was the jobs report strong, but initial jobless claims are also at their lowest since World War II, and more people are leaving their jobs because they have higher confidence in finding a new one.
The quits rate rose 2.1% in September.
But the big news out Friday: The economy added 165,000 jobs in October , compared with expectations of around 70,000, as the unemployment rate edged down to 4.1%, compared with expectations of 4.2%. That's much higher than the average monthly gain of 48,000 over the past 12 months and well above the roughly 30,000 jobs needed to hold employment steady. Over the past three months, payrolls are averaging 137,000.
While job gains were healthy, wages haven't kept pace, though they did catch up last month to the pace of inflation, which grew 3.1%.
"Wage growth had a couple of bad months in part because what's going on in the Iran war made energy prices high," Hassett said, also noting that despite wage growth dips, consumer spending is up significantly. "So people are secure to go out and buy new things because they're confident that they've got their jobs."
The strong jobs report is bolstering expectations that the Federal Reserve will raise rates next month. Markets are pricing in a nearly 80% chance the central bank will raise rates by a quarter percentage point.
Hassett said he isn't worried that the job market is adding to inflation, suggesting the big gain won't add pressure on the central bank to raise rates.
Read more: How jobs, inflation, and the Fed are all related
Referencing recent comments from Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh, Hassett noted that the chairman recognizes that a strong economy and robust job growth don't automatically cause inflation, provided there is "supply side-driven growth" to put "downward pressure on prices."
Hassett said that "reassured" him in thinking about "how hot the economy can get."
Hassett argued the Fed should bear in mind that not all economic growth is driven by higher demand.
"If it's demand driven, then the Fed needs to raise rates. So watch out for inflation. If it's supply driven, you need to look at the inflation numbers and see," he said.
"I think we will watch the inflation number between now and then and they'll make the right call," Hassett added.
Separately, Hassett said he is moving forward with a hearing with Fed governor Lisa Cook to determine whether President Trump has cause to fire her, even in the wake of Democrats winning control of Congress.
"The point is that we're pursuing a process where we want to give Governor Cook every possibility to put her case on the table," Hassett said. "Then a small group of the president's top advisors are going to write a report to the president so that he can have all the evidence to make the decision on what the next move is."
"We can't prejudge how that process is going to work," added Hassett. "We are looking forward collegially to working with Governor Cook and her team."
Trump established a committee last month to investigate allegations against Cook, including mortgage fraud and whether her statements on mortgage documents constituted legal "cause" for her removal from the central bank.
A hearing for Cook was initially scheduled for Nov. 5 but has been pushed back to December.
Any action to remove Cook would likely be met with a lawsuit that would keep her in place. If Cook were ultimately removed, Trump's new appointee would face a Democratic-led Senate that would need to confirm his new nominee.

articles.title_orig: 20 Years of Gears
articles.title_zh: 20 Years of Gears
articles.content_orig:
It’s hard to believe that 20 years ago, Gears of War launched on XBOX 360 and introduced the world to Marcus Fenix, Dominic Santiago, and the genius of putting a chainsaw on a gun.
Since then, a lot has happened.
We’ve released new games, introduced new characters and enemies, and welcomed millions of players into the world of Gears. But when we think about what makes this franchise special, it’s not just the games or the stories we’ve told. It’s the people who have made Gears of War part of their lives.
Over the years, we’ve heard some incredible stories from our fans. Stories of friendships that started in multiplayer lobbies and have lasted for decades. Of campaign playthroughs with fathers or brothers, or groups of friends who made playing Horde together a weekly tradition. Soldiers that have played during military deployments and couples who met playing Gears, fell in love, and eventually got married. Not bad for a game about chainsawing monsters.
And then there are the stories that hit a little harder. Fans who have shared how Gears helped them through a dark and difficult time, whether it was dealing with loss, feeling isolated, or just needing a few hours with Delta Squad to forget about everything else going on in their lives. Sometimes a familiar game and a few friends on the other end of a headset can make a real difference.
For us at The Coalition, these are the stories that matter most.
We’ve always talked about Gears being a franchise built on brotherhood, loyalty, and having each other’s backs. It’s what makes the relationship between Marcus, Dom and the rest of the Gears so important, and it’s been at the heart of the series since the beginning.
But what’s really special is seeing those same values reflected in the community that’s grown around the games. The friendships, the relationships, the shared experiences, and the sense of belonging that comes from finding your people.
It’s an incredible privilege to steward this franchise, to build on the legacy of the creators at EPIC Games, the voice actors and all the creative collaborators who have had a hand in this universe. And to create games that people care so deeply about.
Thank you for making Gears part of your lives, and for letting us be a small part of yours.
To celebrate our 20 th Anniversary, this week we kicked off a 2-week anniversary event in Gears of War: E-Day featuring limited time modes and new rewards. In Versus, play Guardian, where only one leader makes it out alive. And in Horde Siege, try out the For the Queen mode, where the supply cache is disabled, leaving you and the squad to rely on your loadouts.
Tomorrow is the exact date of our anniversary and to celebrate we’re giving away RAAM as a multiplayer character to every Gears of War: E-Day player as a free gift. Just login to claim him instantly.
And beginning December 1, we launch our next Season – titled Legacy – which continues to honor the greatest hits of Gears over 20 years in our maps, modes and multiplayer skins. Season 2 not only brings back some fan favorites from the history of the franchise but lets us reimagine characters in ways we’ve always wanted to see them – like Solemn Memories Dom, whose character skin depicts him in the suit he’s wearing in the famous photo of him and Maria from Gears of War 2.

articles.title_orig: Next year’s iPhone Pro redesign will drop an important button, per leak
articles.title_zh: Next year’s iPhone Pro redesign will drop an important button, per leak
articles.content_orig:
Next year Apple is rumored to have a big redesign coming to the iPhone Pro models, and per a new leak, it may come with the loss of the Action button.
2027 brings the iPhone’s 20th anniversary, and all signs indicate Apple has something special planned. Similar to the debut of iPhone X for the 10th anniversary in 2017, Apple may introduce a bold new iPhone design next year.
New iPhone Pro models are rumored to get quad-curved displays that wrap around the edges for a visually bezel-free appearance. Screen size is expected to increase too.
Now today, a new post from leaker Instant Digital on Weibo says this new design will also come with a loss.
Per the post, the Action button will be removed from next year’s iPhone Pro models. The devices will retain a Camera Control button though, similar to iPhone Duo.
Add a gimmick go jack up the price and then drop the gimmick and keep the price. It’s the Touch Bar all over again.
The leaker says the Action button’s functionality won’t be lost altogether, though. Instead, he says Camera Control will continue to launch the Camera app with a standard press, but a long-press will offer Action button-like functionality.
When iPhone Duo dropped the Action button, some users expressed disappointment that the button’s versatility was lost. Our own Chance Miller, for example, said he would gladly give up Camera Control to keep the Action button.
It sounds like Apple plans to integrate the two, a pattern that will likely apply to the next-generation iPhone Duo and other future models too.
What do you think of Apple’s reported plan for the Action button? Let us know in the comments.
