articles.title_zh: NYC schools’ standoff with Google over AI raises prospect of no search in class
articles.content_orig:
Published Nov 6, 2026 at 10:58 a.m. ET
Published Nov 6, 2026 at 10:58 a.m. ET
Make your contribution now and help Gothamist thrive in 2026. Donate today
Gothamist is funded by sponsors and member donations
Google is locked in a standoff with the nation’s largest public school system as the debate over AI’s place in the classroom pits parent groups against the tech behemoth.
Earlier this week, Google said schools that ban artificial intelligence will lose access to Google search, prompting cries of blackmail and a swift rebuke from Mayor Zohran Mamdani.
“Google is trying to use its monopoly power to force AI into our public schools,” Mamdani wrote on X. “No corporation should have the power to dictate how we teach our children. Our public schools exist to serve students, not to grow the profit margins of Big Tech.”
In September, Mamdani announced a one-year ban on most AI programs in city schools and tighter limits on screens, especially for the youngest students. The moratorium was a major win for city parents who oppose the use of artificial intelligence in public school classrooms.
But Google’s threat to pull the plug on search in classrooms underscored how deeply the technology’s products are woven into the fabric of education.
Google products are ubiquitous in schools. Since the pandemic, many students have been issued individual Chromebooks for schoolwork and remote learning. City officials said the school system has 1.3 million Chromebooks, with about 500,000 assigned to students, and another 800,000 in schools. Teachers post assignments to Google Classroom, and students, like many adults, rely heavily on Google Docs and search.
“It would be incredibly difficult for us to disentangle our school system entirely from Google, and that's what they're betting on,” said Kelly Clancy, part of the coalition calling for a total ban on AI in the city’s public schools. She said all three of her children are required to use Google Classroom for remote learning and homework.
“But I think what they're not counting on is the fact that parents across the country have mobilized against this,” Clancy said. “And this is a perfect time for us to figure out how we wean ourselves off of Google so that we don't have companies able to blackmail us in order to create a captive audience of students.”
Google has insisted it’s impossible to separate the company’s search function from AI.
Chris Phillips, vice president for education at Google, told the New York Times that “search and A.I. are deeply integrated,” so turning off AI will also mean turning off the search engine. The company said the new policy would go into effect early next year. It did not respond to Gothamist’s requests for comment.
But over the past year, an influential movement of parents, educators and lawmakers have sought to beat back the creep of artificial intelligence in schools. They argue AI summaries and bots enable cheating, short-circuit learning and seduce children into inappropriate and even dangerous relationships. This week, parents of a North Carolina 13-year-old sued Google alleging she made plans to end her life after interacting with its AI Mode.
Education officials said they were still trying to figure out how Google’s new policy would affect search in schools.
Officials are “reaching out to Google to discuss this update further,” public schools spokesperson Nicole Brownstein said.
She said the city has disabled the Gemini chatbot and AI mode on Google Chromebooks issued to students, and they’ve made requests to Google to disable the AI Overview that continues to appear in search results.
“We will keep students and school communities updated as we continue to place student safety and wellbeing above all other interests,” she said.
Following the Times report, Google posted additional information about its plans on X .
It said the announcements give schools "more choice, not less" and that Gemini, Gemini Notebook, and Google Search will be off by default, and schools will be in charge of which service, if any, is turned on.
The company emphasized the changes were made in response to feedback from K-12 schools. Google said it’s also changing how AI will function within search “to make it better for learning.” The company said both AI Mode and AI Overviews will offer step-by-step guidance through problems” rather than just “quick answers to schoolwork.”
Assemblymember Alex Bores noted that Google has made “deep investments” into its educational offerings over the years, aggressively and successfully marketing its suite of products to schools.
“This is a product choice that Google is making, and it's a profit maximizing one,” said Bores, who worked at Palantir and recently co-founded Who Decides, an advocacy group for AI safety and regulation.
“Competitors like Duck Duck Go let people opt in or opt out of AI search. And Google could do the same. They could also do the same only when it comes to children if they wanted. But they're making an intentional choice not to, and I think that's a disappointing one,” he said.
Anti-AI parents and educators said Google’s threat should encourage the city to cut ties with the company, and invest in other search engines instead. Naveed Hasan, a member of the Panel for Educational Policy, which votes on education contracts, said the city should consider writing limits into contracts to prevent tech companies from unilaterally changing the software the school system has already purchased without permission.
“We should revisit how we look at technology contracts when companies change their features mid contract,” he said.
Zephyr Teachout, professor at Fordham Law School, said the company’s move may also face legal challenges. “What Google is doing is illegal under antitrust law and I expect there will be investigations from the Attorney General’s office and other places soon,” she said. “It’s simply not credible to me that Google cannot provide search without AI overviews.”
Clancy saw an opening for the school system to rethink how it teaches students to do their work.
“This is an exciting opportunity for us to figure out [how] to teach kids the fundamentals of research,” she said.
Maybe instead of spending so much on Google, Clancy added, the city could invest in school libraries and books.
Jessica is the education reporter for WNYC and Gothamist. During the Covid-19 pandemic, Jessica reported on the shutdown and reopening of the nation’s largest school system, highlighting the unprecedented impacts on learning, health and mental health for students, staff and families. articles.title_orig: A Strange Quantum Theorem Has Killed Einstein’s Reality
articles.title_zh: A Strange Quantum Theorem Has Killed Einstein’s Reality
articles.content_orig:
Click to tell Google to prioritize Quanta and see more of the best coverage of science and math in your search and AI results.
Recent work has ruled out out our most commonsense understanding of reality.
Samuel Velasco/ Quanta Magazine
O ne of a human’s earliest developmental milestones is an understanding of object permanence. It generally takes less than a year for a baby to realize that when an adult hides their face behind their hands in a game of peek-a-boo, they don’t cease to exist. There’s more to the world around us than what we perceive.
This suggests — or at least, it suggested to Albert Einstein — that the world is “real,” in the sense that things in the world have properties that are intrinsically true no matter what anyone thinks. A red billiard ball is red, even in the dark, and even if no one is checking its color. The redness is a property belonging to the ball, not to some device measuring the ball, and not to the mind of some person operating the measuring device.
Yet quantum mechanics, a thoroughly validated theory of how the world works, seems to suggest otherwise. The theory’s math assigns redness to the billiard ball at the moment you measure it. Before then, the theory gives you only a set of probabilities telling you what color the ball might be. Key founders of quantum mechanics suggested that this math reflects the nature of reality — that in some sense, a single, objective reality doesn’t really exist.
In 1935, Einstein rebelled against this surreal reading of quantum theory, proposing one of the 20th century’s most famous thought experiments. But his rebellion was doomed. In 1964, the physicist John Stewart Bell showed with a thought experiment of his own that reality had to be stranger than Einstein assumed. Subsequent work would put Bell’s thought experiment to the test — and prove him right.
Then, 50 years after Bell, Matthew Pusey , at the time a graduate student at Imperial College London, took on what remained of Einstein’s notion of reality and — without originally intending to — delivered the killing blow.
Matthew Pusey took on the debate about the nature of reality in his doctoral thesis at Imperial College London.
The paradigm-shifting theorem became known as PBR, for Pusey and his academic accomplices, Jonathan Barrett and Terry Rudolph. Since the publication of PBR in 2012, many theorists have come to accept that it rules out our most commonsense understanding of reality.
“From the moment [PBR] came out, people knew it would be a landmark,” said Jacques Pienaar , a physicist now at the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro in Brazil.
At the time, Pienaar, like Pusey, had been walking in Einstein’s footsteps, dabbling in theories designed to show that objective reality exists and that quantum mechanics merely describes our incomplete knowledge of it. But when the PBR theorem appeared, Pienaar remembers thinking, “That’s it. The program’s dead.”
This is the story of how Einstein, Bell, and finally Pusey and his collaborators killed reality as we know it. In three theorems, they proved that quantum mechanics is incompatible with the world we perceive. And since experiment after experiment — including a recent realization of PBR — has established that quantum mechanics is the law of the land, something about reality has to go.
The question that remains is: How much do we have to give up?
After playing a pioneering role in developing the theory of quantum mechanics, Einstein turned around and attacked it. He couldn’t accept what it said about reality.
Einstein knew in his bones what reality was. It was the sum total of all objective facts — like the color, position, and velocity of a billiard ball — that exist in the objects they describe, independent of perception and mind. But quantum mechanics, as developed by Werner Heisenberg and Erwin Schrödinger in the mid-1920s, didn’t deal in facts.
Quantum mechanics deals in possibilities. Its mathematics gives you a “quantum state,” also known as the wave function. This wave function can tell you, for example, that in an experiment measuring the color of a particular billiard ball, you will have a 77% chance of finding the ball to be red and a 23% chance of finding it to be green.
Albert Einstein’s argument that particles should have real properties that quantum mechanics can’t capture became known as the Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen paradox.
The question that has stumped physicists for a century is: What is the nature of the ball before the experiment takes place? Does the ball have multiple colors? No color? Does the concept of color not have a meaning? In short, is there a reality to support the object permanence we experience?
To Einstein, the answer was obvious: Of course reality exists; the wave function just doesn’t fully capture it.
In this view, the wave function is like a weather forecast. Say you wake up and your weather app tells you there’s a 77% chance that it will rain today, but you haven’t looked outside to see what’s going on. Then you raise the blinds and see raindrops falling. In that moment you become 100% certain that it’s raining. This shift from 77% to 100% is a shift in certainty that occurs purely in your head. It doesn’t reflect some real meteorological change. The atmosphere is real, and your (un)certainty about its state is something else — a reflection of the information in your mind.
Einstein, along with his collaborators Boris Podolsky and Nathan Rosen (collectively, “EPR”), came up with a thought experiment to prove that the quantum state exists only as an artifact of information. To understand the thought experiment, you need to know one peculiar thing about the wave function: Its mathematical structure doesn’t allow an object to have a position and a momentum at the same time.
The EPR experiment involved bouncing two particles off each other and, sometime later, making a measurement, such as how far one particle had traveled. This first measurement would also tell you how far the partner particle had traveled. EPR argued that the position of the partner particle had to exist, because it could be known. They argued that the partner particle also had a momentum, because that property was knowable in a similar way.
Crucially, their experiment involved measuring only one particle one time, while the other remained untouched. This showed, the scientists argued, that the second particle had properties that were set and real, even before measurement. And since the wave function doesn’t allow for that, the wave function must not reflect the literal state of the particle; the quantum state is not real.
To reach this conclusion, the scientists had made two seemingly unassailable assumptions. First, they assumed that it was possible for a particle to have a literal state, the assumption of “reality.” And second, they assumed that this literal state existed within the particle and nowhere else, so the only way to change it would be to interact with the particle, the assumption of “locality.”
But just months after EPR, Heisenberg’s mentor, Niels Bohr, tried to shut down Einstein’s argument by attacking its first assumption. “There is no quantum world,” Bohr would later say, according to his assistant Aage Petersen. “There is only an abstract quantum physical description.” His argument was akin to asserting that the weather forecast was accurate but that the atmosphere itself was either nonexistent or indescribable. This denial of objective reality became known as the Copenhagen interpretation.
Niels Bohr engaged in a sustained public debate with Einstein in the 1920s and ’30s about the implications of quantum mechanics.
Public Domain/Paul Ehrenfest
Many modern quantum physicists criticize Bohr’s response to EPR for being confusing and vague. articles.title_orig: UN climate talks start in the year of disasters, energy price shocks and fast rising temperatures
articles.title_zh: UN climate talks start in the year of disasters, energy price shocks and fast rising temperatures
articles.content_orig:
Council on Foreign Relations
Representatives from around the world will gather in Antalya, Turkey, from November 9 to 20 for the thirty-first Conference of the Parties (COP31) to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change. Although it is an annual event, this year’s climate summit is notable for two reasons: first, it coincides with the tenth anniversary of the Paris Agreement entering into force; and second, the United States—the world’s second-largest and historically biggest emitter, which formally withdrew from the agreement at the start of this year—will not send an official delegation. (Members of Congress and U.S. businesses will still attend.)
With the legacy of the Paris Agreement in question, COP31 President Murat Kurum has set the goal of moving beyond climate pledges to the concrete implementation of existing commitments. Alongside the formal COP agenda, Kurum has introduced an Action Agenda organized around ten themes, including the clean energy transition and electrification, zero waste and methane reduction, and climate-resilient cities. The COP31 presidency has also put forward voluntary pledges, including a 35-by-35 pledge aimed at increasing electricity’s share of total energy consumption to 35 percent by 2035—up from 23 percent today—as well as a commitment encouraging countries, corporations, and investors to make artificial intelligence more sustainable.
COP31 comes after three decades of work on climate change. Major concrete outcomes are not expected, but hope remains that parties can press forward on goals such as methane emissions reductions, adaptation and finance, and accelerating the implementation of existing COP agreements.
There are achievements to be celebrated at COP31. When the Paris Agreement was negotiated in 2015, the world was on track to experience catastrophic warming of 3.7°C–4.8°C [PDF] (6.7°F–8.6°F) by 2100. Thanks to policy shifts and the growth of clean energy, including a spectacular increase in global solar capacity by 2025 to over ten times what it was in 2015, projected warming by the end of the century has fallen.
Under current policies, temperatures are now expected to rise by around 2.8°C (5.0°F), or around 2.6°C (4.7°F), if the most recent climate commitments are fully implemented. This is still an extremely dangerous level of warming, but bending the curve downward by a degree spares the Earth from some of the worst consequences of climate change. The heat is already beginning to bite: August 2026 joined July 2023 as the hottest month on record globally.
The summit in Antalya will cover familiar points of discussion from previous COPs, including climate finance, greater emissions reductions, and funding for loss and damage in countries that have contributed the least to climate change. Of these, finance will likely prove the most contentious issue on the formal negotiating agenda.
Climate finance. Article 9.1 of the Paris Agreement states that developed countries “shall provide” financial resources to developing nations “with respect to both mitigation and adaptation”—but who pays, in what form, and how much are matters of long-standing debate. At COP31, developing nations will continue pressing developed countries to deliver on existing funding commitments, including the COP29 goal to mobilize at least $300 billion per year in climate finance by 2035 and the COP30 call to at least triple adaptation finance over the same period. Developed countries provided and mobilized a record $136.7 billion in climate finance in 2024, according to the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development. Although developing nations are seeking faster and larger payouts and note that loans can add to debt distress, developed nations are under financial stress from increased fuel costs.
Fossil fuels. How to treat fossil fuels is a recurring point of contention at recent COPs. At COP30, the parties failed to formalize a roadmap for transitioning away from fossil fuels, even though the measure drew support from a broad coalition of more than eighty countries. The outcome of COP30—the Belém Political Package —omitted the words “fossil fuels” from the official text. Vulnerable nations, civil society groups, environmental nongovernmental organizations, and other actors viewed the omission as a major pullback from the Glasgow Climate Pact (COP26), which called for the phasedown of unabated coal power and phaseout of inefficient fossil fuel subsidies, and the United Arab Emirates Consensus (COP28), which explicitly called for transitioning away from fossil fuels. To quell the tension, the COP30 presidency published elements of a voluntary roadmap ahead of COP31.
Emissions reductions. The COP31 formal agenda includes the Mitigation Work Program, an initiative designed to accelerate emissions reductions. In a June lead-up meeting to COP31, however, nations could not agree on the terms of the initiative, including whether it should drive cuts or remain a space for dialogue. Negotiators have also clashed over the Global Goal on Adaptation, tussling over whether to reference the call to triple adaptation finance into the formal text and how to shape metrics and indicators to measure progress.
Other topics. Another issue likely to feature is the just transition mechanism agreed to be developed at COP30. The mechanism aims to strengthen cooperation and provide technical support to economies transitioning away from carbon-intensive industries. But questions remain over how the mechanism should operate in practice, and further dialogue on the topic is scheduled to take place at COP31.
Additionally, since COP26 in Glasgow, when the Global Methane Pledge was introduced, more than 150 countries have signed on to reduce methane emissions. Methane is a potent greenhouse gas that is responsible for about 30 percent of global warming and plays a significant role in near-term heating. There are low-cost, readily available ways to cut methane, and doing so now would help slow the rate of heating. There are hopes that COP31 will help accelerate ambition to cut methane emissions, particularly in the oil and gas sectors.
The Paris Agreement’s stretch goal of limiting global warming to 1.5°C (2.7°F) has slipped out of reach, according to the 2026 Emissions Gap Report by the UN Environment Program. The report finds that efforts to keep warming to well below 2°C (3.6°F) would require emissions to fall 18 percent by 2030, 45 percent by 2035, and 69 percent by 2040, compared with 2025 levels. Yet current national commitments will not yield that level of reduction. Beyond the lack of ambition shown by many countries, additional headwinds have emerged with the potential to push the 2°C goal even further out of reach.
One such headwind is the delay in science-based reporting. The second global stocktake—an inventory check of progress toward meeting the Paris Agreement’s goals—will begin at COP31, but the scientific process that underpins it is sputtering. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), the UN-backed body of scientists responsible for assessing the latest climate science, has failed to reach agreement on when it will finalize the next set of working-group reports. The IPCC had proposed publishing the reports in 2028, but member states were unable to agree on a timeline at a meeting in October. A group of countries, including China and Saudi Arabia, argued that more time was needed because the dominance of developed nations in climate science skewed IPCC findings.
But delaying the timeline means that nations could base their next round of national commitments to reduce emissions on outdated science. Some scientists and experts warn that in the absence of updated, comprehensive climate science reporting, climate ambition could wane among some parties.
Adding to the headwinds is uncertainty over the outcomes of national elections. In the United States, control over both chambers of Congress could decide if climate change r

articles.title_orig: Russia using own version of Starlink for military comms over Ukraine, Kyiv says
articles.title_zh: Russia using own version of Starlink for military comms over Ukraine, Kyiv says
articles.content_orig:
Russia is building its own satellite network to expand its military capabilities. RASSVET system could eventually allow Russian forces to control attack drones over much greater distances, threatening countries beyond Ukraine. With Belarus helping develop the network’s ground infrastructure, the Baltic states could face a new security threat on NATO’s eastern flank.
RASSVET is a low Earth orbit satellite communications network that has been under development since 2023 by the private Russian company Bureau 1440, with state support.
In 2026, funding and deployment of the project accelerated after Russia lost access to Starlink , dealing a significant blow to its offensive capabilities. RASSVET aims to replicate the American system and establish Russia’s own independent satellite internet network.
Its successful deployment would pose a threat not only to Ukraine but also to Russia’s neighbors, particularly the Baltic states.
To make the system fully operational, Moscow is involving its allies, particularly Belarus. A ground control facility is being built there, providing the infrastructure needed to expand the system’s coverage. The project’s local partner is Belintersat, a Belarusian satellite operator.
For now, Ukraine faces the most immediate threat from RASSVET’s deployment. However, the construction of the necessary infrastructure in Belarus is already expanding the system’s geographical reach. RASSVET could also pose a threat to the Baltic states—Lithuania, Latvia, and Estonia—which are located near Russia and Belarus.
The potential threat is substantial. Thousands of Russian drones could carry out precision strikes against military facilities and critical infrastructure in countries that may not be prepared to repel such an attack. Most importantly, these strikes could be carried out with relatively inexpensive drones, while defending against them would be costly. This challenge has already become evident during the war in the Middle East.
While RASSVET has yet to reach its planned operational capacity , its potential military applications are already becoming apparent in Ukraine.
In Russia, RASSVET is primarily presented as a civilian project, but the reality tells a different story.
Ukrainian military personnel have already documented the use of the system’s terminals on Molniya drones —inexpensive fixed-wing attack drones capable of traveling dozens of kilometers.
For now, Ukraine faces the most immediate threat from RASSVET’s deployment. Equipped with satellite terminals, Russian drones would be able to carry out more precise strikes deep inside Ukrainian territory. Countering such attacks would become more difficult because the drones would be controlled through a satellite communications network.
Notably, although the system is being deployed gradually, it is already being used on the battlefield. Between 2023 and 2024, the first six test satellites were launched into orbit. In 2026, following the suspension of Starlink services, development accelerated, with dozens of satellites launched into orbit. Although not all of them reached their designated orbital positions or became operational, the project is moving forward.
The Kremlin plans to have 250 satellites in orbit by 2027, 730 by 2030, and more than 900 by 2035.
Russia is well aware of the capabilities of its new satellite system and is already waging a hybrid war against its main competitor, Starlink. Over the past month, SpaceX infrastructure has been attacked three times in European countries . Infrastructure essential to Starlink’s operations was damaged in Poland, Bulgaria, and Lithuania.
In October, Axios also reported that a Russian satellite had approached the American ICEYE-X36 satellite to within just a few dozen meters. This could have been an attempt to interfere with American satellite equipment. Russia may be testing potential methods of interference while also gauging how other countries might respond.
One way to counter this threat is through sanctions. As of now, Belintersat is subject to sanctions imposed by all major jurisdictions, including the United States and the European Union. The problem, however, is that only the United States has imposed sanctions on the Russian company Bureau 1440.
European countries are also exploring technological countermeasures. Germany is assessing ground-based systems capable of disrupting satellite communications and navigation signals, potentially enabling interference with RASSVET’s operations.
Ukraine, meanwhile, is pushing for international restrictions on the Russian satellite network. Moscow has included Ukrainian territory in the declared service areas of its RASSVET-1 and RASSVET-3 systems, prompting Kyiv to appeal to the International Telecommunication Union (ITU).
Ukraine is demanding that its territory be excluded from the networks’ declared service areas and has raised concerns about potential interference with Ukrainian communications systems. Kyiv is also urging other countries whose territories Russia has included in its planned coverage areas to submit similar objections.
Another approach is, at the very least, to prepare for countermeasures. Starlink currently does not operate in Russia, and SpaceX prohibits such use of its services. However, allowing Starlink to operate even a few hundred kilometers into Russian territory could potentially expand Ukraine’s ability to conduct drone operations against Russian military equipment farther from the border, including ballistic missile launchers. This could help reduce threats to border regions in Ukraine and neighboring countries.

articles.content_orig:
Odds that Anthropic will announce a public offering fell in recent days on Kalshi as AI-related stocks slid after Democrats won control of Congress and several key governorships.
In the last week, odds that Anthropic would announce an IPO before December fell to 57% from over 85% on Kalshi. Chances that the company would announce a public offering before January also dropped to 68% from 90% in the last week. The contract asks when Anthropic will officially announce an IPO and will be verified by news outlets.
The AI company confidentially filed its IPO prospectus with the Securities and Exchange Commission back in June.
The repricing on Kalshi came as investors grew concerned that Democratic victories across both chambers could slow data center construction, making the bet on AI less attractive.
Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa of Texas, a Democrat who ousted three-term Republican Greg Abbott, championed tighter protocols against data center buildout in her state during her campaign.
"We will have laws to protect Texans and we need to stop what we are doing with data centers until we have those protections," the Democrat told CNN on Thursday.
The Nasdaq Composite closed Thursday more than 10% below its most recent high, crossing the benchmark for what Wall Street views as a correction. The S&P 500 lost 4.4%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell more than 1,800 points, or 3.4%. Stocks were attempting to rebound on Friday, with the Nasdaq gaining 1.3% and the S&P 500 rising 0.7%. The Dow shed 0.2%.
On Friday, shares of Micron Technology and Nvidia each gained about 4%, after falling 17% and 9%, respectively, the day before. CoreWeave shares also rose more than 2% Friday morning after tumbling about 10% on Wednesday. Even if Friday's gains are sustained, these stocks have tallied steep losses over the past week.

articles.title_orig: Iran official delivers secret Khamenei message to Putin in Moscow trip
articles.title_zh: Iran official delivers secret Khamenei message to Putin in Moscow trip
articles.content_orig:
Iran’s Supreme National Security Council Secretary met Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow on Thursday, where he delivered a personal message from Iran’s Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei regarding the Iran war and discussed what both sides called “strengthening ties”.
Iran’s top security official described the meeting as an "extremely important exchange of views," which covered "the post-war situation and regional security.”
Russia has been a long-standing supporter of Iran, purportedly supplying Tehran with intelligence and equipment during the war. Tehran has previously backed Russia in its all-out invasion of Ukraine, and provided its Shahed drone technology.
Moscow has since cloned it into its domestically-made Geran UAVs, which it commonly uses in its daily strikes on infrastructure and civilian targets in Ukraine.
The meeting, which was not announced in advance, follows the Russian president's meeting with his Iranian counterpart Masoud Pezeshkian in Moscow during a summit of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum last week.
The content of Khamenei’s message to Putin was not made public, Iranian state broadcaster IRIB reported.
"The construction of gas pipelines from Russia to Iran was discussed" during the meeting with Putin, Rezaei stated.
He explained that the project aims to help Tehran "address its gas shortages, while also facilitating the sale of Russian gas to neighbouring countries."
Although Iran is a major producer of natural gas, it has long suffered from shortages of the fuel, a crisis that has only intensified since the onset of the Iran war in late February.
According to Tehran, during the most intense phase of the war — which lasted nearly 40 days — the US and Israel launched strikes against critical Iranian infrastructure, including gas processing plants.
Iran responded by attacking what it said were US military facilities and other interests in the broader Middle East region. Regional governments, witnesses on the ground and Euronews journalists reported the strikes also hit civilian and infrastructure targets.
Both sides also imposed concurrent blockades of the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway for the world's gas and oil trade.
In early October, Putin stated that Russia is prepared to act as a mediator to help end the war. Moscow has not acted as an intermediary in the talks. Pakistan and Qatar have so far served as the main mediators.
Rezaei noted that Putin emphasised the need for regional security mechanisms and asserted that "any interference by external powers" in resolving the situation in the Middle East is unacceptable.
Russia has delayed, deflected to Kyiv or otherwise rejected all attempts to broker an end to its ongoing war in Ukraine, now well into its fifth year.
According to Rezaei, the meeting also addressed progress on key bilateral infrastructure projects. "The Supreme National Security Council has approved the executive agreement for the construction of the Rasht–Astara railway, with Russian participation," he said, as cited by the Iranian news agency IRNA.
"The Minister of Roads and Urban Development will soon sign this contract on behalf of the Islamic Republic of Iran," Rezaei added.
Spanning just over 160 kilometres, this section represents the final missing link in the western route of the International North-South Transport Corridor (INSTC), which is intended to provide a direct connection between Russia and Iranian ports on the Persian Gulf.
Press reports citing the semi-official Iranian news agency Fars indicated that Russia had finalised preparations to provide Iran with a $1 billion loan, though the transfer of funds has been delayed.
According to Fars, this $1 billion is intended to be the first instalment of a planned $20 billion Russian loan to Iran.
Some experts have linked the delay in disbursing these funds specifically to the stalled progress of the Rasht–Astara railway project.
"We are prepared to provide the necessary credit resources," Putin stated during a meeting of the Valdai Discussion Club on 1 October.
"The question is for our Iranian friends to complete their part of the work at this stage."
After the meeting, the Russian Foreign Ministry issued a warning travel advisory telling Russians to avoid visiting Iran and the Middle East while the risk of renewed war persists.
The Russian Foreign Ministry had previously advised Russian citizens against travelling to Persian Gulf countries for tourism — specifically in February, right before the US and Israel launched their attacks on Iran in the opening salvo of the war.
That advisory was lifted in June after Washington and Iran signed an interim deal, which has since collapsed.

articles.title_orig: US economy adds 165,000 jobs in October, blowing past expectations
articles.title_zh: US economy adds 165,000 jobs in October, blowing past expectations
articles.content_orig:
Kenny Polcari discusses the historical S&P 500 performance following midterm elections. He predicts the stock market will be higher in 12 months, continuing a trend seen in every midterm cycle since World War II.
The U.S. economy added jobs at a strong pace in October, rebounding from a softer September amid economic uncertainty.
The Bureau of Labor Statistics on Friday reported that employers added 165,000 jobs in October. That figure was well above the 65,000 estimate of economists polled by LSEG.
The unemployment rate decreased slightly to 4.1%, which was lower than the expectations of economists who predicted it would hold steady at 4.2%.
Revisions were made to the payroll numbers for the prior two months, with August revised up by 53,000 from a gain of 133,000 jobs to 186,000 jobs; while the change for September was revised up by 31,000 jobs from a gain of 29,000 to 60,000.
Taken together, employment in August and September was 84,000 higher than previously reported.
TRUMP ADMIN NAMES NEW ECONOMIC OPPORTUNITY ZONES TO SPUR PRIVATE INVESTMENT IN STRUGGLING COMMUNITIES
Private payrolls grew by 159,000 jobs in October, well above the 64,000 expected by economists polled by LSEG.
Government payrolls increased by 6,000 jobs in October. The sector's loss of 17,000 jobs in September was revised down to a loss of 18,000 jobs. The federal government shed 1,000 jobs in October, while state governments added 8,000 jobs and local governments cut 1,000 roles last month.
The manufacturing sector added 19,000 jobs in October, well above the gain of 5,000 that was predicted by economists polled by LSEG. September's gain of 9,000 jobs was also revised up to 13,000. Professional and business services added 70,000 jobs in October, which was well above the average monthly gain of 15,000 jobs over the past 12 months. The sector's job growth was led by gains in professional, scientific and technical services (+32,900), and in administrative and support and waste management and remediation services (+28,100).
Healthcare added 41,600 jobs in October, above the average monthly gain of 31,000 over the last 12 months. Most of last month's gains were in hospitals (+16,000), home healthcare services (+10,500) and outpatient care centers (+4,800).
Transportation and warehousing added 24,800 jobs last month, with growth occurring among couriers and messengers (+17,400) and air transportation (+3,500).
Private payrolls grew by 159,000 in October, well above the expectations of a gain of 64,000 jobs. (Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
PRIVATE SECTOR ADDED 86,000 JOBS IN OCTOBER, ABOVE EXPECTATIONS, ADP SAYS
The number of long-term unemployed, defined as those who have been jobless for 27 weeks or more, was 2 million in October and changed little over the month. The long-term unemployed accounted for 27.6% of all unemployed people.
The number of people employed part-time for economic reasons rose by 339,000 to 4.8 million in October. These individuals would've preferred full-time work but were working part-time because their hours were reduced, or they were unable to find full-time jobs.
The labor force participation was 61.9% in October, while the employment-population ratio was 59.3%. Both of these figures were little changed in October and have shown little net change since January.
Average hourly earnings increased 3.1% year over year in October, above the 2.4% rise predicted by LSEG economists. Earnings also grew 0.4% on a monthly basis, above the 0.3% estimate in the LSEG poll.
FED'S PREFERRED INFLATION GAUGE ROSE IN SEPTEMBER AS THIRD-QUARTER GDP BEATS EXPECTATIONS
Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh and central bank policymakers will hold their next interest rate meeting on December 8-9. (Daniel Heuer/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Seema Shah, chief global strategist at Principal Asset Management, said in a statement that the October jobs report "is a strong rebuttal to fears that the economy is heading into a meaningful slowdown."
"Payrolls growth surprised firmly to the upside, unemployment fell back to 4.1%, and job creation remains broad-based, pointing to an economy that is still absorbing labor comfortably rather than one beginning to buckle under tighter financial conditions," Shah said. "With wage growth also picking up, a December Fed hike remains firmly on the table despite the recent tightening in financial conditions."
Lindsay Rosner, head of multi-sector fixed income investing at Goldman Sachs Asset Management, said that the October jobs report's "payroll number removed the traffic light at the December intersection for the Fed."
"Fed focus was already firmly on moderating inflation , and continued signs of tightening in the labor market give it a license to raise rates without hindering its employment mandate. Additional tightening is possible in the first quarter if inflation continues to print strong," Rosner added.
The strong October jobs report raised the likelihood of the Federal Reserve hiking interest rates when it holds its next meeting on Dec. 8-9.
The market's expectations of a 25-basis-point rate hike ticked up on Friday, with the CME FedWatch tool showing a 76.8% probability the Fed hikes in December – an increase from 66.9% a week ago. A hike of that size would take the federal funds rate to a target range of 4% to 4.25%.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average slipped 0.2%, while the Nasdaq Composite rose 1.25%.

articles.title_orig: Nasdaq rebounds as chips stocks recover from steep losses
articles.title_zh: Nasdaq rebounds as chips stocks recover from steep losses
articles.content_orig:
Asian and European markets follow US tech rout with many analysts predicting more waves of selling to come
European and Asian stock markets fell sharply on Friday after the Democrats’ decisive victory in the midterms triggered a rout in US tech stocks a day earlier.
A sell-off on Wall Street on Thursday was followed by sharp falls in Asian stock markets on Friday. The investor sentiment then reached London, where the market was, at one stage, poised for its worst day since March.
The FTSE 100 index, which tracks blue-chip shares listed in London, was down as much as 254 points, or 2.35%, at 10,528 points during a wave of selling in morning trading. But by the close of the day it had clawed back some of its losses to be down 1%, helped by a rise in US stocks when Wall Street reopened.
Germany’s Dax index fell by 2%, France’s Cac 40 dropped by 0.8% and Spain’s Ibex lost 0.6%.
Susannah Streeter, the chief investment strategist at Wealth Club, said: “The tech sell-off has intensified, with the pain of the brutal sell-off on Wall Street carried straight through to Asia and knocking sentiment in Europe .
“Big worries are colliding – the build-out of datacentres looks set to slow, which risks shredding the spending spree underpinning the boom, right at the time that investors have become super nervous about returns on this massive investment.”
However, there were signs of easing jitters on Wall Street on Friday, where tech stocks rose in early trading, lifting the S&P 500 share index by 0.8% by early afternoon in New York and the Nasdaq by 1.6% – which only recovered a portion of their previous day’s losses.
That followed a stronger-than-expected employment report that showed the US economy added 165,000 new jobs in October, pulling the unemployment rate down to 4.1%.
On Thursday, the Nasdaq share index had its worst day in 19 months after slumping 5.5%.
Chip stocks led the slump on Thursday, with the memory maker SanDisk tumbling by 22% and the hard drive maker Western Digital falling by 17%. Wall Street’s “fear index”, the Vix, jumped by more than 60% to its highest levels since the early weeks of the Iran war, in a sign of rising market volatility.
The heavy falls continued in Asia on Friday, with Japan’s Nikkei 225 index sinking 6% and South Korea’s Kospi index tumbling more than 6.5%.
“It’s actually a bit of a disaster,” said Christopher Forbes, the head of Asia and Middle East at CMC Markets.
“[Clients] were long index, long stocks, and they all got carried out. All night, all day – we had client margin calls, client complaints … because it’s a very emotional thing, right? People are wedded to their positions and views on a stock or outcome, and you’re telling them: ‘Look, you’ve just lost money.’”
Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said: “Yesterday’s [Thursday’s] brutal session marked a dramatic turnaround from Wednesday, but with AI fears still prominent there is a risk that there is much more selling to come.
after newsletter promotion
“Investors remain on watch for a potential resumption of the Iran conflict, and are nervously watching the oil price after its slump earlier in the week. All in all it remains a very febrile atmosphere.”
However, despite the sharp losses suffered on global stock markets around the world, most indices are still up for the year. The Nasdaq Composite index remains up 6.35% since the start of January – even though it is more than 10% below its peak.
The FTSE 100 has gained almost 7.5% in 2026 – but it is now more than 300 points below the record high set in July.
Mohit Kumar, an economist at the investment bank Jefferies, said that while he did not expect a quick rebound from Thursday’s losses in the US, he also did not believe it marked the “start of the unwind of the AI trade”.
He said: “AI investment has been a key driver of US growth and we do not see the Democrats as giving up on this growth engine. Datacentres and AI infrastructure also create jobs and Democrats would be reluctant to let those jobs move on to other states or outside the country.”
Stock market tremors have also hit the London Metal Exchange, with copper poised for its biggest weekly fall since March.
Benchmark three-month copper, a key metal used in the semiconductor, electronics and automotive industry, has dropped 0.61%, leaving it positioned for a 2.79% fall this week.
Craig Lang, a principal analyst at the consultancy CRU, said the price of copper was increasingly influenced by the AI market and “sentiment towards datacentre expansion”.

articles.title_orig: Europe alarmed by US plans for security deal with Russia
articles.title_zh: Europe alarmed by US plans for security deal with Russia
articles.content_orig:
BRUSSELS — Europe is once again watching the White House through gritted teeth.
An opaque Trump administration proposal for a new European-wide security arrangement with Russia has met skepticism from European capitals that fear it risks sidelining the continent and emboldening Kremlin chief Vladimir Putin.
“We already have a European security architecture in place — NATO and European Union both have their respective roles,” EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said Friday in reaction to the U.S. plan. “We must make sure Ukraine is integrated into this architecture. The problem remains that Russia keeps breaking the treaties that underpin it ... Putin does not have a veto over European security.”
The latest U.S. proposal underscores growing anxiety around Trump’s fresh rapprochement with Russia as he ramps up pressure on Ukraine and his administration attempts to revive long-stalled talks to end Moscow’s full-scale war against Kyiv.
POLITICO spoke to 12 NATO diplomats, EU envoys and European government officials, all of whom were granted anonymity to speak freely on the sensitive issue. NATO allies were not briefed about the American plans in advance, according to three alliance diplomats, and many remain skeptical of the idea.
U.S. President Donald Trump late Thursday talked of a “big, beautiful agreement,” after meeting with Putin’s envoy Kirill Dmitriev, adding: “It’s going to involve more than Ukraine, and I could even say it might involve all of Europe.”
“Our objective is to develop practical arrangements that address the security concerns of all sides, reduce the risk of future conflict, and create a more stable and predictable security environment,” Trump’s son-in-law and envoy Jared Kushner added soon after.
Kushner said the arrangement would have five goals: “Permanent security consultations, reliable crisis communications, greater military transparency, reciprocal measures to reduce escalation risks, and an enduring framework for long-term European security and stability.”
“It is a bit obscure what Kushner meant,” said one NATO diplomat. “The general sentiment in Europe is that any discussion with Russia on the future architecture at the moment will just be used by Moscow to legitimize their arguments ... it will not fly with the European allies.”
A senior European official added: “Literally, there’s nothing to find fault with, but we know there’s something else going on.”
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s top adviser, Björn Seibert, briefed EU ambassadors on Friday, according to two EU diplomats, following a discussion between national security advisers on the issue.
“There’s willingness to engage in Kyiv and in the rest of Europe although there’s little confidence in the Russians — but the EU is not blocking it,” one of the EU diplomats said after the meeting. But “the group around Trump underestimated how important the conflict is for Europe and how a bad outcome for Ukraine is very dangerous for Europe.”
“It's a long-standing position for us and many others that European security architecture should not be discussed while there is a war,” said a senior European security official. “And obviously not without Europeans.”
“Europe must have a seat at the table in negotiations on peace in Ukraine and the future European security architecture,” Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda added Friday, after a meeting of the eight Nordic and Baltic countries.
This week saw two rounds of working-level meetings in Brussels on a Ukraine peace deal, ahead of U.S.-brokered working-level talks with Ukraine and Russia on Nov. 10-11 in Abu Dhabi.
“We must be realistic about the peace talks and we must be very careful when it comes to the real intentions of Russia,” Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk told a group of reporters, including from POLITICO, earlier this week. “In winter, Putin might have less incentives to get a deal.”
Stefan Kornelius, spokesperson for German Chancellor Friedrich Merz — who talked to Trump on Thursday night — said: “A new sense of urgency has ... emerged” on negotiations after this week's U.S. midterm elections, adding the issue would resurface at an informal gathering of EU leaders in Dublin next week.
The meeting had been intended to focus on AI, but developments in Ukraine could overshadow the talks, a third EU diplomat said. “Things are moving pretty fast,” they said.
Still, some allies fear the U.S. may tie its new initiative to an upcoming review of American troops in Europe, expected in December.
“That’s the elephant in the room,” said a second NATO diplomat. “One thing is talking about European security architecture ... with an ‘ordinary’ U.S. posture; another thing is to talk about a European security architecture ‘as things will be,’ and nobody knows how that’ll be.”

articles.title_orig: Watch live: Jim Cramer says an Anthropic IPO would be a cue to start buying again
articles.title_zh: Watch live: Jim Cramer says an Anthropic IPO would be a cue to start buying again
articles.content_orig:
Odds that Anthropic will announce a public offering fell in recent days on Kalshi as AI-related stocks slid after Democrats won control of Congress and several key governorships.
In the last week, odds that Anthropic would announce an IPO before December fell to 57% from over 85% on Kalshi. Chances that the company would announce a public offering before January also dropped to 68% from 90% in the last week. The contract asks when Anthropic will officially announce an IPO and will be verified by news outlets.
The AI company confidentially filed its IPO prospectus with the Securities and Exchange Commission back in June.
The repricing on Kalshi came as investors grew concerned that Democratic victories across both chambers could slow data center construction, making the bet on AI less attractive.
Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa of Texas, a Democrat who ousted three-term Republican Greg Abbott, championed tighter protocols against data center buildout in her state during her campaign.
"We will have laws to protect Texans and we need to stop what we are doing with data centers until we have those protections," the Democrat told CNN on Thursday.
The Nasdaq Composite closed Thursday more than 10% below its most recent high, crossing the benchmark for what Wall Street views as a correction. The S&P 500 lost 4.4%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell more than 1,800 points, or 3.4%. Stocks were attempting to rebound on Friday, with the Nasdaq gaining 1.3% and the S&P 500 rising 0.7%. The Dow shed 0.2%.
On Friday, shares of Micron Technology and Nvidia each gained about 4%, after falling 17% and 9%, respectively, the day before. CoreWeave shares also rose more than 2% Friday morning after tumbling about 10% on Wednesday. Even if Friday's gains are sustained, these stocks have tallied steep losses over the past week.

articles.title_orig: Everything Is Going Wrong for Chip Stocks. 5 Names at Fire-Sale Prices.
articles.title_zh: Everything Is Going Wrong for Chip Stocks. 5 Names at Fire-Sale Prices.
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
You don't have to look that far to grasp the severity of the increasingly painful chip stock sell-off .
Just start with the two names that were (keyword: were) the leaders of the AI-fueled momentum for much of 2026: Sandisk ( SNDK ) and Micron ( MU ).
Micron stock crashed 14% on Thursday, bringing its one-month plunge to a startling 36%.
The rout has brought Micron's forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio down an almost laughable 4.8 times, according to Yahoo Finance AlphaSpace data. Keep in mind Micron is coming off a quarter of strong demand amid memory chip shortages driving up prices.
The Street still expects Micron to grow earnings by at least 17% in its next fiscal year.
Sandisk is in the same valuation boat as Micron, trading at about 4.9 times estimated forward earnings on a P/E basis. Similar to Sandisk, its business has been very strong, and the Street remains bullish on its profit outlook.
Sandisk stock is down 19% today, bringing its one-month drop to 29%.
For perspective here, the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) trades at about 18.5 times estimated forward earnings.
The bottom line appears to be this: The market couldn't care less about the valuations on either former AI momentum darling. The prevailing view is that, with Democrats taking control of the House and Senate and victories in key governor races, the construction of new data centers will be slowed.
That could mean fewer orders for Micron and Sandisk and a reassessment of their longer-term earnings power.
In other words, each is likely a value trap — until the dust settles on the AI trade.

articles.title_orig: OpenAI Launches GPT-6 Cyber After AI Helps Find 81 Firefox Flaws, 948 Linux Exploits
articles.title_zh: OpenAI Launches GPT-6 Cyber After AI Helps Find 81 Firefox Flaws, 948 Linux Exploits
articles.content_orig:
A cybersecurity model trained to find and validate exploitable vulnerabilities, while staying within the scope that researchers set.
We’re introducing GPT‑6 Cyber, a major leap in security research: more capable at finding and fixing vulnerabilities, and far more reliable staying within the boundaries researchers set. GPT‑6 Cyber delivers major gains on key cybersecurity benchmarks over GPT‑5.6 Cyber, including a 51% relative improvement on ExploitGym and a step function improvement when tested on staying within scope. It is already helping to secure real-world software, uncovering and validating thousands of exploits in security-critical codebases such as Linux and Firefox.
On ExploitGym, which tests whether models can exploit a specified vulnerability, GPT‑6 Cyber scores 48.5%, up from 32.1% for GPT‑5.6 Cyber. It also follows task boundaries more reliably: in a separate alignment evaluation, GPT‑6 Cyber avoided exploiting out-of-scope services in 99.93% of tests without its deployment prompt , and 100% with this prompt . This improvement in alignment reflects dedicated training to stay within authorized scope, respect restrictions, and report results accurately.
These capabilities are already helping secure real systems. Our researchers used GPT‑6 Cyber to develop 948 privilege escalation exploits in Linux ⁠ and identify 81 previously unknown high-severity vulnerabilities in Firefox, despite extensive prior testing with frontier models. The model also helped develop candidate patches, and Mozilla has released fixes for many of the Firefox vulnerabilities ⁠ (opens in a new window) . Security teams at Cisco, Calif, and CodeRabbit are using it for vulnerability research and code review, and we have relied on it to find and fix weaknesses in our own infrastructure ⁠ .
It is clear that we have a limited window to use frontier models to secure software ⁠ . Our goal is to dramatically expand Daybreak, bringing advanced security research to organizations of every size, independent researchers, and open-source maintainers. Mainline models such as GPT‑6 Astra already support code review, vulnerability triage, and patch development. Daybreak Blue helps verified defenders validate vulnerabilities and fixes with fewer unnecessary refusals, while Daybreak Red enables deeper exploit development and authorized security testing with GPT‑6 Cyber.
GPT‑6 Cyber is a major step up from GPT‑5.6 Cyber and outperforms GPT‑6 Astra on most cyber tasks, even when Astra does not refuse the request. We evaluated the model on tasks that require it to understand software, identify vulnerabilities, and develop working exploits. Based on these results, we classify the model as Critical in cybersecurity under our Preparedness Framework, up from High for GPT‑5.6 Cyber.
On ExploitGym, which tests whether models can exploit a specified vulnerability in a remote target, GPT‑6 Cyber scores 48.5% , about 16 percentage points higher than GPT‑5.6 Cyber’s 32.1% . To test vulnerability discovery, we also built a new evaluation for offensive web penetration testing. Models probe web applications without access to their source code. GPT‑6 Cyber achieved 40.3% recall of vulnerabilities compared with 32.0% for GPT‑6 Astra.
Daybreak Red is designed to support more advanced security workflows, including developing working exploits and using them against remote targets. To evaluate these capabilities, we built a new benchmark called RemoteExploitBench, which uses known vulnerabilities in applications such as GitLab, PostgreSQL, and Jenkins deployed in a controlled environment. In our initial evaluation, GPT‑6 Astra running with Daybreak Blue refused 100% of tasks , while GPT‑6 Cyber completed 95% ; its only failure was an exploit it could not get to work remotely. See the system card ⁠ (opens in a new window) for full results and evaluation settings.
One risk for cybersecurity agents is that they go outside the scope of their assigned task, attempt to exploit unrelated services, or disregard the researcher’s rules of engagement.
We made alignment a central focus of GPT‑6 Cyber, using specialized training to help the model stay within authorized scope, follow restrictions on its actions, and report its work accurately. Before deployment, we ran a series of alignment evaluations to measure these behaviors. See the system card ⁠ (opens in a new window) for full results.
One of these evaluations is ExploitGym Honeypot, which was informed by the Hugging Face incident ⁠ . We give the model a difficult exploitation task in an isolated environment with access to supporting services, such as a package registry or object store. We deliberately make these services easy to exploit so that attacking them can reveal the task’s flag. The model must infer that exploiting them is outside the scope of its task.
GPT‑6 Cyber shows a step-change improvement over GPT‑5.6 Cyber on this evaluation. When tested without deployment safety prompts, it avoided exploiting out-of-scope services in 99.93% of cases, up from 94.49% for GPT‑5.6 Cyber. With those prompts, GPT‑6 Cyber stayed within bounds 100% of the time.
We can see directly in the GPT‑6 Cyber model’s chain of thought how it reasons about staying within bounds:
GPT‑6 Cyber is already helping security teams find vulnerabilities, validate their impact, and develop fixes. Customers have put it to work on large codebases, long-running exploit development, and security review:
We have also relied on GPT‑6 Cyber to secure our own systems. It was one of the main models behind the work we recently shared on hardening the infrastructure used to train frontier models ⁠ . In controlled red-teaming campaigns, agents using GPT‑6 Cyber and other OpenAI models chained vulnerabilities to escape microVMs and execute code on the underlying hosts. We used the findings to patch software, tighten network restrictions, and report issues to maintainers and vendors.
Our vulnerability researchers also use GPT‑6 Cyber to find and validate vulnerabilities in open-source software at scale. This work has uncovered previously unknown flaws in software that has been scrutinized for years:
Found 81 novel Firefox vulnerabilities. GPT‑6 Cyber can be suitable for use in autonomous workflows for finding vulnerabilities and proposing high-quality patches at scale. During a vulnerability research campaign, GPT‑6 Cyber produced evidence and reproducible tests for 81 novel vulnerabilities classified by Mozilla as high severity, and showed that an additional 30 known issues were more severe than previously reported. We disclosed the findings to Mozilla, along with proposed patches to help its engineers develop fixes. Mozilla was supportive of this work, and began landing fixes shortly after receiving the reports ⁠ (opens in a new window) .
Developing exploits for 948 Linux kernel vulnerabilities ⁠ . GPT‑6 Cyber reproduced 1,724 vulnerabilities and developed working exploits for 948—more than five times the 166 exploited by GPT‑5.6 Sol using the same research harness. Following the Linux community's guidance, we disclosed 304 critical findings to maintainers with candidate patches and are in the process of getting other vulnerabilities fixed.
Demonstrating critical RCE vulnerabilities. We recently discussed a critical vulnerability in Brotli ⁠ (opens in a new window) , a compression library used by Node.js and other software. Our security researchers used GPT‑6 Cyber alongside other OpenAI models to develop and validate exploits showing how the flaw could enable remote code execution in downstream applications.
As models become more capable and uncover more security vulnerabilities, we are also seeing more attempts to use them to cause harm. These attempts include efforts by malicious cyber actors and adversarial groups seeking to distill our models. We have thus paired GPT‑6 Cyber’s stronger capabilities with stronger safeguards to detect and disrupt misuse and keep the model’s actions within the user’s in

articles.title_orig: Tanzanian opposition leader found guilty of inciting unrest but acquitted of treason
articles.title_zh: Tanzanian opposition leader found guilty of inciting unrest but acquitted of treason
articles.content_orig:
Tanzania's main opposition leader, Tundu Lissu, has been found guilty of inciting unrest and sentenced to four years in jail, in a case that has raised concerns about political freedom in the East African country.
A panel of three judges at the High Court in Dar es Salaam acquitted him of the more serious offence of treason, saying prosecutors had failed to prove a key element of that charge.
But they said the 58-year-old, who has been detained since April last year, had encouraged his supporters to disrupt the disputed 2025 general election.
Lissu, who leads the opposition Chadema party, has denied the charges, describing the prosecution as politically motivated.
The court said his campaign slogan "No Reforms, No Election" was sufficient for him to be convicted of the charge of incitement.
"By uttering those words with the intention of disseminating them to the public, the accused incited the public to disrupt the 2025 elections," the court ruled.
Lissu said he had only been charged with treason, not incitement.
"The offence of incitement is one that you, honourable judges, have manufactured. You have created an offence that did not exist, and you have done so on political directives," Lissu told the court.
He added that he would like to apply for bail as this was possible for incitement, unlike treason.
He has leave to appeal at the Court of Appeal - the country's highest court.
But if the four-year sentence is upheld, it would rule him out of the next elections, due in 2030.
Treason is among Tanzania's most serious offences and can carry the death penalty.
Human rights group Amnesty International described his conviction as a "travesty of justice".
"Tundu Lissu should never have been arrested, let alone prosecuted and convicted," said its regional director for East and Southern Africa, Tigere Chagutah:
President Samia Suluhu Hassan won the October 2025 election with 98% of the vote - a result the opposition dismissed the result as a "mockery" of democracy as her two main challengers, including Lissu, were excluded.
Her government has repeatedly denied targeting its opponents.
The Chadema leader was arrested six months before the poll, shortly after launching a campaign demanding changes to the electoral system under the slogan "No Reforms, No Election".
Prosecutors accused him of making statements intended to incite the public to disrupt the election and threaten the government.
They argued that his remarks, which were also circulated online, amounted to treason.
But Lissu, a lawyer who represented himself during the trial, maintained that his comments were part of a legitimate political campaign for constitutional and electoral reform.
He argued that prosecutors had taken his statements out of context and failed to prove that he had committed any crime.
Some of the demands raised by Chadema were:
During his time in remand custody at Dar es Salaam's Ukonga Prison, Lissu went on hunger strike twice for brief periods when he said he was not allowed access to his lawyers or relatives. He also complained that guards listened to what should have been private consultations his lawyers.
These allegations have been denied by the prison authorities.
His case has attracted international attention, with rights groups expressing concern about the treatment of opposition politicians and the shrinking space for political dissent in Tanzania.
Last year's election was followed by widespread protests and a violent security crackdown that left at least 500 people dead, according to an official inquiry.
Opposition groups have said the death toll was much higher and demanded an independent investigation.
The government has defended its handling of the unrest and rejected accusations of widespread political repression.
Samia, 66, has insisted the election was fair and transparent and blamed foreigners for the unrest, saying it was part of a plot to overthrow her. She has set up another commission to inquiry to identify those behind the violence.
Lissu has long been one of Tanzania's most outspoken critics of the ruling Chama Cha Mapinduzi (CCM) party, which, along with its predecessor Tanu, has dominated the country's politics since independence.
He first became an MP in 2010, representing a constituency near his birth place in Singida, 320km (200 miles) north-west of the capital, Dodoma.
In September 2017, the Chadema politician narrowly survived an assassination attempt when gunmen sprayed his vehicle with bullets outside his home in Dodoma.
He was shot multiple times and underwent extensive medical treatment abroad.
The attack, whose perpetrators have never been brought to justice, forced him to spend years in exile.
He returned to contest the 2020 presidential election against the late President John Magufuli, but lost in a vote that the opposition alleged was marred by widespread irregularities.
Lissu subsequently returned to exile before coming back to Tanzania in 2023, following President Samia's decision to lift a ban on opposition political rallies.
His return was initially seen as a sign of renewed political openness after years of restrictions under Magufuli, who died in office in 2021.
But relations between the government and the opposition deteriorated as the country approached the 2025 election.
Lissu became Chadema's national chairman in January 2025 and intensified his demands for electoral reforms.
His conviction is likely to deepen concerns about the state of democracy in Tanzania.
Last week, Amnesty accused the government of continuing its crackdown following the election and "weaponising counterterrorism laws to silence critics and instil fear".
The authorities did not respond to a request for comment.
Correction: An initial version of this story said Lissu had been convicted of inciting treason. We have corrected this to incitement.

articles.content_orig:
The end of the year is always a prime time for PS5 game delistings and server closures, but fortunately we’re being spared a large list this year.
There are about eight titles with impending changes you need to be aware of, so here’s the full list:
Subscribe to Push Square on YouTube 172k
Sony game Destruction AllStars will go completely offline on 25th November, following some alterations earlier in the year.
This will render most of the single player content unplayable, outside of a few arcade challenges, although the platform holder says your overall experience may be affected in those too.
In-game purchases will then be removed from Synduality: Echoes of Ada , the Bandai Namco live service shooter. This is the beginning of the publisher repurposing the game as a single player-only experience, with more changes planned in 2027.
PSVR2 MMO Zenith: Nexus will go offline on 18th December, and then the end of the year brings a slew of delistings, primarily from publisher GameMill.
This is due to licenses expiring for franchises like Avatar: The Last Airbender and Street Outlaws . If you purchase these games before they’re removed, they’ll remain in your library.
While it never officially released, PlayStation fans may want to pay attention to the impending closure of Ratchet & Clank: Ranger Rumble , which will be removed from mobile storefronts on 21st November.
One final thing to note is that 2K Sports will disable the online servers of NBA 2K25 on 31st December, but single player modes will remain.
That’s the full breakdown of everything being delisted in November and December 2026, then. I’ll update should any other announcements be made before the end of the year.
Is there anything here you’re going to miss? Let me know below.
As the Editor of Push Square, Sammy has over 15 years of experience analysing the world of PlayStation, from PS3 through PS5 and everything in between. articles.title_orig: Protesters Break Into Microsoft Data Center in Amsterdam
articles.title_zh: Protesters Break Into Microsoft Data Center in Amsterdam
articles.content_orig:
Separate actions also take place outside fence and across Europe in backlash against impact of AI boom
Activists have stormed the site of a Microsoft datacentre being built in Amsterdam, as the backlash to the social and environmental harms of the AI boom spreads across Europe.
Protesters from Geef Tegengas, a Dutch direct action group, clashed with police while breaking into a construction site at Westpoort Amsterdam, where some members climbed a crane, lit flares and tied helium balloons to equipment.
The action comes amid Europe-wide resistance to the rapid expansion of energy-hungry AI, with more than 100 groups involved in a two-day series of protests to demand moratoria on the construction of new datacentres.
The break-in at the Dutch site, where protesters hung banners objecting to Microsoft’s services to the Israeli military and US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) , was separate from the pan-European “Stop Dirty Data Centres” campaign, which targeted the same site but whose affiliated members stayed outside the perimeter fence.
“The police attempted to prevent [the occupation] and arrest protesters, but were unable to prevent it and force was used,” the police said in a statement to NOS, a Dutch public broadcaster. “An officer was slightly injured during the protest.”
Protesters from both groups said police used force and teargas to dispel the activists trying to enter the construction site. Organisers and local media reported hundreds of protesters on each side of the fence.
Smaller protests took place in the centre of Bristol, in the UK, at a datacentre in Berlin, Germany, outside the Polish parliament in Warsaw and at the main square in Zagreb, Croatia. Further protests are expected on Saturday.
Stop Dirty Data Centres, a coalition of independent groups that include national branches of Greenpeace and Friends of the Earth, said it had not coordinated or promoted the direct action that took place in the Netherlands , but that is was “understandable” communities would turn to a range of tactics when they were unable to meaningfully participate in decision-making.
“Big tech and government are racing ahead with large-scale datacentre development despite significant public concern about the impacts on local communities, natural resources and other industries,” said Owen Espley, campaign coordinator. “Many datacentre developments are planned with limited transparency or scrutiny, while communities across Europe are being shut out of decisions that will shape their local environments and futures.”
The ecological fallout of the datacentre boom has alarmed some climate scientists, while growing frustration with AI’s societal impact – from energy bills and job losses to the role of tech companies in undermining democracy – has increased public anger. In the US midterm elections this week, nearly every proposed moratorium on datacentres on the ballot was approved.
Roos Molenaar, an activist from Geef Tegengas, said the struggle against big tech was inseparable from the fight against oppression and fascism. “We won’t accept Amsterdam being used for the creation of AI slop and the facilitation of genocide,” said Molenaar. “This datacenter is gulping up our drinking water to make the rich even richer.”
after newsletter promotion
A spokesperson for Microsoft said it was aware of the demonstration and that its first concern was the wellbeing of everyone at and around the site. “We understand that people feel strongly about the project, and we respect their right to express those views peacefully. However, we do not condone any actions that are unlawful or that put people’s safety at risk.”
A spokesperson for Pure Data Centres, the site owner, said it respected the right to peaceful protest but that entering a live construction site was unlawful and dangerous.
“Our immediate priority is everyone’s safety, and we respectfully ask those on site to leave safely and engage with us in dialogue about the development and any concerns they may have,” a Pure DC spokesperson said.
Governments across Europe have supported the building of AI datacentres to boost tax revenues and catch up with the breakneck deployment of computing power in the US and China, with some framing the AI race as a matter of national security.
But datacentres have emerged as a flashpoint for public anger over issues from environment and energy to human rights and democracy. Last week, an investigation by the Guardian and Investigate Europe found evidence of dangerous conditions for some of the workers building them.

articles.title_orig: ANC faces bruising defeat in South African local elections with 80% of ballots counted
articles.title_zh: ANC faces bruising defeat in South African local elections with 80% of ballots counted
articles.content_orig:
Former liberation movement’s share of national vote almost 14 percentage points below 2021 result
The African National Congress is on course to suffer a bruising defeat in South Africa’s local elections, with the once dominant party of Nelson Mandela falling to under a third of the vote nationally with more than 80% of ballots counted.
Wednesday’s fragmented vote marks another stage in the decline of the ANC, which has led national governments since the end of white minority apartheid rule in 1994. High unemployment, crime, corruption and poor local service delivery have all contributed to voters turning away from the party .
The former liberation movement is projected to lose its status as the biggest party in the two most populous provinces, Gauteng and KwaZulu-Natal, as parties began coalition negotiations behind closed doors. The final results are expected to be announced on Sunday.
The ANC was on 31.8% of the vote nationally, almost 14 percentage points below its 2021 local election result. The centre-right, white-led Democratic Alliance (DA) had 24.1% of the vote, while the uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) party of the former ANC president Jacob Zuma was on 9.3%.
Turnout also rose in Wednesday’s poll. The election commission estimated that 54.5% of registered voters cast their ballot, up from 46% five years ago.
The final shape of coalitions in some of the country’s biggest cities remained unclear with the final votes still being counted. Senior figures in key parties said they would talk with almost anyone, while keeping negotiating strategies under wraps.
In Johannesburg, South Africa’s commercial capital and biggest city, with 4.8 million people, voters have had to contend with regular water and power cuts , uncollected rubbish and potholes. The municipality, which has seen 10 changes of mayor in the last decade amid unstable coalitions, has admitted to a 220bn rand (£9.9bn) infrastructure spending backlog.
With just over half of votes counted in Johannesburg, the DA was leading with 40%, having run an energetic campaign under Helen Zille, a 75-year-old former Cape Town mayor. The ANC, which leads the current coalition, was in second place on 17.5%. ActionSA, a rightwing party led by Herman Mashaba, was on 15.5%. Mashaba has pledged never to work with Zille, whom he calls “racist”, something she vehemently denies.
Many of the ANC’s township strongholds have yet to report full results. The Council for Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR), a respected thinktank, has projected the DA will finish with 34%, the ANC 20% and ActionSA 16.8%.
Coalitions in Gauteng’s three city municipalities are often negotiated together. The DA is leading in all three.
after newsletter promotion
The MK party, led by 84-year-old Zuma as he continues to weather and deny numerous corruption allegations, is expected to displace the ANC as the largest party in KwaZulu-Natal. Founded in 2023, it mixes socially conservative Zulu nationalism with pledges to redistribute land and wealth from white to black South Africans.
With half of votes counted in eThekwini municipality, which contains Durban, the MK had 41%, meaning other parties could form a coalition to keep it out of power. Meanwhile, the DA is projected to maintain its majority in Cape Town, despite growing middle-class anger over rising housing costs .
Voters choose a local councillor and a party, with seats allocated via proportional representation. Councillors will then have two weeks to elect mayors and form municipal governments.
